Here, we demonstrate a versatile one-pot synthesis to fabricate a large variety of 2D perovskite heterostructures based on different halides and/or metal cations. Exploiting sequential crystallization of different 2D perovskites and tuning the composition and injection events of the materials, enables the design of diverse heterostructure architectures, including multiple heterojunctions. We obtain heterostructures with high crystalline quality, multicolor emission, and optical coupling between the different heterostructure regions. We foresee that the design freedom of our method will stimulate the development of novel optoelectronic devices where electronic band engineering is crucial.

title: Cathode-Driven Aluminothermic Fronts Amplify Thermal Runaway in Lithium-Ion Batteries.
abstract: NA: Thermal runaway in lithium-ion batteries often develops from a local failure into a spatially propagating high-temperature front. Here, we show that oxygen-bearing cathode materials and metallic aluminium can form self-sustained, glowing, cathode-driven aluminothermic fronts in inert gas as a heat-amplification pathway relevant to severe thermal runaway. Using a mesoscale platform based on semi-1D composite bars, we isolate this interfacial redox chemistry from gas-phase combustion, internal short-circuit heating, and other coupled cell-failure processes. Nickel-rich layered oxide/aluminium bars sustain aluminothermic-front propagation in argon, with velocities of the same order of magnitude as reported thermal-runaway fronts. By varying aluminium loading, reaction atmosphere and cathode chemistry, we show that front propagation depends on aluminium fuel supply, the oxygen-donor capability of the cathode, and access to oxygen gas. Crystalline phase and chemical-state analyses reveal Li-Al-O/Al-O products together with reduced or reconstructed transition-metal species, supporting cathode-to-aluminium oxygen transfer as the underlying redox pathway. For a representative 2-Ah cell, energy-audit calculations indicate that the aluminium-cathode reaction gives a potential heat scale equivalent to about half of the stored electrical energy. These findings identify cathode-Al redox chemistry as an internal heat-amplification mechanism that should be considered in battery hazard assessment and high-energy-cell safety design.

title: Ionization-State-Directed Sulfonate-Rich Buried Interfaces Enable Durable High-Efficiency Perovskite Solar Cells and Modules.
abstract: NA: Proton-triggered degradation at the buried interface severely undermines the operational stability of inverted perovskite solar cells (PSCs). To address this issue, this work develops an ionization-state-directed sulfonate approach using sodium 2,2'-disulfanediyldiethanesulfonate (DDANA). The pre-deprotonated sulfonate terminals grant DDANA strong coordination with lead sites and drive its spontaneous aggregation at the perovskite and self-assembled monolayer interface, forming robust multisite binding with the perovskite lattice. The enriched sulfonate groups build favorable interfacial dipoles to optimize energy level alignment and facilitate hole transport. The immobilized sulfonate groups act as conjugate-based sites to competitively capture protons, while the disulfide skeleton enables reversible iodine-redox to scavenge corrosive iodine species under operational stress. Dissociated sodium (Na+) ions embed into lattice interstices and release residual tensile strain. As a result, DDANA-modified inverted PSCs achieve a champion efficiency of 27.38% (certified 27.13%). The strategy extends seamlessly to flexible devices and rigid large-area modules, delivering efficiencies of 25.88% and 23.33%, respectively. Moreover, the DDANA-modified devices retain 98.9% of their initial efficiency after 1000 h of maximum power point tracking and 97.4% after cycling diurnals. This work establishes sulfonate ionization-state engineering as a versatile molecular design platform for constructing chemically robust buried interfaces toward efficient, stable, and scalable perovskite photovoltaics.

title: Threshold-Voltage Ion Sieving in Ultrathin Polymeric Membranes for Energy-Efficient Lithium Extraction.
abstract: NA: Biological ion channels achieve multi-ion discrimination through parallel chemically distinct channel types, each optimized for a single ion species. Replicating this within a single synthetic membrane has remained beyond reach, for conventional membrane resistance blocks the bonding energy difference between different ions. Here we show that an ultrathin polymeric membrane (ca. 8.56 nm) bearing aligned angstrom-scale porphyrin pores, fabricated by interfacial superspreading, reduces internal resistance sufficiently and achieves simultaneous multi-ion discrimination. Under a microvolt-scale applied voltage, the membrane separates six ion species across three valence groups. In particular, the membrane exhibits anomalous selectivity for Li+, with a threshold voltage Vt ≈ 400 mV which is 370 mV above the nearest competitor. Applied to lithium extraction from low-quality brines, a two-stage device achieves >98% recovery at 1.1 × 10-4 Wh g-1 (Li), three orders of magnitude below conventional electrodialysis. This membrane architecture offers a broadly applicable design principle for energy-intensive separations in which resolving ions of similar charge and size is the critical challenge.

title: Cross-Scale Decoupling of Mechanics and Kinematics in Chiral Tensegrity Metamaterials.
abstract: NA: Compression-torsion metamaterials (CTMs) that break spatial inversion symmetry face persistent trade-offs among large deformation capacity, intrinsic stiffness, and fatigue durability. Crucially, boundary rotation induced by axial compression complicates integration with rotationally constrained engineering interfaces. Here we introduce a chiral three-rod tensegrity cell (CTTC) paradigm that addresses these conflicts through a cross-scale dual-decoupling strategy. First, mechanical decoupling at the unit-cell scale separates macroscopic shape-morphing from large local material strain: a heterogeneous rigid-flexible architecture channels global compression into kinematic rod displacement and uniform elastic-network stretching, achieving 97° torsion at Level 0 and only 4.87% peak-force degradation over 10 000 cycles at Level 3. An integrated geometric interlocking reconfigurator further enables post-fabrication programmability of stiffness and strain-normalized twist ratio (RT-S). Second, kinematic decoupling at the assembly scale localizes torsional deformation as a boundary-decoupled internal rotational mode, while maintaining external interfaces in pure translation. This cross-scale framework establishes a deployable paradigm bridging metamaterial physics and robotic systems operating in geometrically constrained environments.

title: Ambipolar Fiber Amplifiers for Highly Sensitive Biosignal Detection.
abstract: NA: Biological signals are inherently weak and susceptible to noise, making in situ signal amplification critical for high-fidelity sensing. Electronic fibers offer unique advantages for conformal and scalable biointegration; however, fiber amplifiers are seldom reported due to the lack of suitable semiconducting materials that combine balanced ambipolar transport, scalable fiber fabrication, and high device performance. Herein, we report the first single-component ambipolar fiber platform based on a newly designed polymer, P(gTDPP-TQ), which combines balanced p- and n-type transport, low-cost synthesis, and continuous fiber fabrication. Fiber processing enhances molecular ordering and charge transport, yielding record-high µC* and gm,norm among reported semiconducting fibers, enabling high-performance fiber amplifiers with a high voltage gain of up to 150 V V-1 and low operating voltages down to 0.5 V. These fiber amplifiers enable high-fidelity electroencephalogram signal amplification over 20 times and sensitive cortisol sensing with a record-low detection limit of 3.7 fM. This work establishes a general ambipolar fiber platform for integrated bioelectronic amplification and sensing.

title: Interface-Directed Two-Dimensional Growth of Non-Layered NiO on MoS2 Under Coupled External Fields.
abstract: NA: The controlled growth of two-dimensional (2D) non-layered transition metal oxides remains a key challenge in low-dimensional material synthesis. Achieving atomically precise construction of 2D structures requires a fundamental understanding of how external fields and interfacial interactions govern nucleation and growth processes. In this work, amorphous NiOx (a-NiOx) was deposited onto monolayer MoS2, and its transformation into crystalline 2D NiO nanosheets was directly visualized in situ using environmental transmission electron microscopy. The electron beam induces the decomposition of a-NiOx into mobile NiOx species, which migrate and nucleate on MoS2, demonstrating the synergistic roles of the electron beam and thermal field in NiO cluster formation and interface-dominated epitaxial growth. Combined notch-filtered imaging and theoretical calculations reveal that Ni-O units preferentially attach at the NiO/MoS2 interface to form one-dimensional growth fronts, while oriented attachment proceeds via nanosheet rotation, interfacial fusion, and defect-mediated reconstruction, culminating in lattice relaxation into a single-crystalline structure. High-throughput selected-area electron diffraction further uncovers the modulation of external fields on the multi-path structural evolution of NiOx. This work establishes an in situ strategy to resolve nucleation and growth pathways of 2D heterostructures, enabling active control over the 2D growth of non-layered metal oxides and advancing deterministic atomic-level construction.

title: In Situ Probing of Small-Molecule Electrolysis Using Ambient-Pressure X-Ray Photoelectron Spectroscopy.
abstract: NA: Electrocatalytic small-molecule conversion addresses the need to couple renewable electricity with sustainable fuel and chemical production, yet challenges remain in resolving the dynamic gas/solid/liquid interfaces that govern catalytic activity, selectivity and stability. A key challenge is to correlate catalyst structures, reaction intermediates and local interfacial environments under comparable operating conditions. Ambient-pressure x-ray photoelectron spectroscopy (APXPS) provides surface-sensitive and chemically specific information on catalyst chemical states, interfacial species and local electrostatic environments at the same working interface, enabling direct correlations between catalyst evolution and reaction intermediates. We offer a forward-looking review of APXPS for probing gas/solid/liquid interfaces in small-molecule electrolysis. We discuss three categories of electrochemical XPS/APXPS configurations: quasi-in situ XPS, in which electrochemically treated catalysts are transferred under protected conditions for post-reaction analysis; thin-electrolyte-film (dip-and-pull) APXPS, which probes a potential-controlled interface through a nanometer-scale liquid film; and membrane-based APXPS, which accesses catalyst-ionomer-electrolyte interfaces. We introduce present-day challenges in electrochemical APXPS and describe a vision towards more realistic operating conditions, higher time resolution and multimodal measurements integrated with theoretical and data-driven spectral analysis. These developments provide potential avenues to establish reliable structure-intermediate-environment relationships in the further development of small-molecule electrocatalysis.

title: Smart Luminescent Materials: From Basic Luminophores to Stimuli-Responsive Luminescent Systems.
abstract: NA: Smart luminescent materials (SLMs) represent an emerging class of intelligent optical systems that can convert external stimuli into adaptive and programmable photonic outputs. By integrating molecular photophysics with dynamic structural regulation, SLMs enable precise modulation of emission intensity, wavelength, polarization, lifetime, and energy conversion pathways with high spatiotemporal controllability. Recent advances in molecular engineering, supramolecular assembly, and hierarchical material design have driven a transition from conventional luminescence switching toward multifunctional systems featuring multilevel, multistimulus, and information-enriched optical responses. This review provides a comprehensive and mechanism-oriented overview of recent progress in SLMs across diverse material platforms, including solution-phase systems, solid-state materials, dynamic hydrogels, chiral circularly polarized luminescence (CPL) systems, and lanthanide-doped upconversion nanoparticles. Particular emphasis is placed on how external stimuli regulate excited-state electronic structures, molecular conformations, supramolecular organizations, and hierarchical architectures to achieve adaptive luminescent behaviors. In addition, emerging strategies for stimuli-responsive CPL regulation and intelligent photon conversion based on upconversion nanomaterials are highlighted, demonstrating how molecular-level control can be translated into dynamic optical functionalities. Finally, current challenges and future opportunities are discussed toward the rational design of next-generation smart luminescent materials for applications in information security, wearable electronics, soft robotics, biophotonics, and intelligent photonic devices.

title: In Situ Bulk Passivation and Carrier Transport Modulation in Te-TeOx Films Enable Low-Noise Monolithic Near-Infrared Imagers.
abstract: NA: Near-infrared (NIR) imagers are essential for applications ranging from material sorting and autonomous driving to biomedical diagnostics, yet their performance is often limited by severe carrier recombination and high dark current. Here, we demonstrate a low-noise NIR photodiode based on Te-TeOx nanocrystalline-in-matrix films, in which the surrounding oxide matrix provides in situ bulk passivation and enables the modulation of carrier transport to balance carrier loss and extraction. This approach reduces trap density, suppresses recombination, and prolongs carrier lifetime, while controlled oxide incorporation tunes the optical bandgap and interfacial offsets of the heterojunction photodiode, resulting in spectral response spanning the visible and NIR regions with low dark current. The resulting photodiodes exhibit a low dark current of 9.70 nA cm-2 at a bias of -10 mV, a detectivity of 3.85 × 1012 Jones and an ultralow detectable power of 1.35 pW for NIR photodetection. The strategy is compatible with direct monolithic integration with readout integrated circuits, enabling a 256 × 256 focal-plane imager with excellent pixel uniformity. It further supports high-quality focal-plane imaging in both visible and NIR regions, as well as solution identification and imaging through smoke.

title: A Noninvasive Approach to Study Localized Forces in 3D Epithelia.
abstract: NA: Epithelial tissue integrity and remodeling rely on mechanical coupling between cytoskeletal organization and adhesion complexes, but their orchestration in three-dimensional (3D) epithelia remains unresolved. Here, we introduced a noninvasive strategy to locally probe forces within 3D epithelial tissues. We engineered elastic polyacrylamide (PAAm) microbeads with cell-like size and mechanical properties, enabling their integration into tissues. PAAm microbeads were spontaneously engulfed by the tissue, establishing an intrinsic interface. This allowed bead deformation to be directly correlated with local cytoskeletal architecture and adhesion organization, visualized through high-resolution imaging and quantitative 3D computational reconstruction. Using this approach, we demonstrated that localized mechanical perturbations trigger cytoskeletal remodeling while preserving tissue polarity. We further identified extracellular matrix composition as a key determinant of bead-tissue interactions. At the bead-cell interface, cells assembled tension-bearing focal adhesions and actin stress fibers. Quantitative analysis of bead deformation revealed sub-cellular scale patterns of cell-bead interaction forces, which correlated with the localization of cytoskeletal elements. Our findings extend previous traction force microscopy observations to 3D, revealing coordinated, spatially heterogeneous forces specifically at the cell-bead interface. Taken together, this enabled us to dissect the interplay between cellular processes and tissue mechanics in a noninvasive way in 3D model systems.

title: Buried CdSe Sacrificial Layer Driving Phase Evolution and Crystallization Kinetics Enables 14.78%-Efficient DMF-Based Kesterite Solar Cells.
abstract: NA: During selenization, the inherent transport lag of Se from the film surface to the buried Mo/precursor interface causes early-stage Se deficiency in the bottom region, creating a depth-dependent crystallization lag that limits the homogeneity of Cu2ZnSn(S,Se)4 (CZTSSe) absorbers. Here, we evaporate an ultrathin CdSe sacrificial layer at the Mo/precursor interface of N,N-dimethylformamide (DMF)-derived CZTSSe absorbers. This layer is rapidly consumed at the onset of selenization, providing an in-situ Se supply at the buried interface and effectively bypassing the intrinsic transport delay from the surface. The locally supplied Se initiates early-stage bottom selenization and promotes the conversion of Cu2SnSe3-related intermediates toward CZTSSe while suppressing their persistent accumulation, enabling rear-side nucleation and grain growth to commence substantially earlier than in the conventional surface-dominated process. Meanwhile, the redistributed Cd2+ partially substitutes Zn2+ sites, reducing defect-assisted recombination and enhancing carrier transport and extraction. The optimized device achieves a champion efficiency of 14.78% with a certified efficiency of 14.30%, establishing a new benchmark for DMF-derived kesterite solar cells. This work demonstrates that prepositioning a sacrificial Se-containing component at the buried interface to enable in situ release of Se offers a viable pathway for coordinating phase evolution and improving multinary chalcogenide absorber quality.

title: Coordination Bridges in Confined-Water Domains Enable Partially Desolvated Zn2 + Transport in Aqueous Zinc-Ion Batteries.
abstract: NA: Zinc-ion batteries (ZIBs), owing to their intrinsic safety and cost competitiveness, are attracting significant interest as next-generation energy storage system (ESS) technologies. However, their commercialization is severely hindered by poor cycle stability, primarily originating from dendritic Zn growth and parasitic hydrogen evolution. To address these challenges simultaneously, we design and integrate a multifunctional polymeric protective layer incorporating amide and imidazolium functional groups. The zincophilic amide groups facilitate ion transport by providing stable Zn2+ binding sites, whereas the hygroscopic imidazolium groups establish a confined-water domain that regulates local solvation dynamics. Within this domain, water molecules transiently stabilize Zn2+ and act as a coordination bridge during ion migration, yet their mobility toward the electrode surface is restricted. This dual functionality increases the Zn2+ single-ion conductivity 6.55-fold and reduces the hydrogen evolution rate by 79.1%. Consequently, Zn//Zn symmetric cells exhibit markedly extended cycling lifetimes of up to 2200 h at 1 mA cm-2 and 1 mAh cm-2. When applied to Zn-I2 full cells, the protective layer enables stable operation over 4000 cycles with >85% capacity retention, even under a practical areal capacity of 3.6 mAh cm-2. These findings highlight a robust interfacial strategy to realize long-duration, high-capacity aqueous ZIBs for grid-scale energy storage.

title: Non-Selective Suppression of Cation and Anion Crosstalk from an Anode Perspective.
abstract: NA: Metal fluoride and sulfur cathodes are appealing for their abundance and high capacity but are plagued by severe electrode crosstalk. This occurs when transition metal cations or polysulfide anions dissolve and shuttle to the anode, causing corrosion and rapid capacity fade. Herein, we propose an anode-centric mechanism utilizing a Na-rich nanoalloy (NaxSn) anode that achieves simultaneous kinetic regulation and physical shielding, suppressing cation and anion crosstalk at both the source and destination. The ultrafast kinetics of the NaxSn alloy elevate the Damköhler number (Da), a descriptor quantifying the competition between conversion and diffusion, thereby ensuring these species are rapidly reduced at the cathode prior to outward diffusion. Concurrently, this nanoalloy induces the formation of an ultrathin, robust Na2O-rich solid electrolyte interphase that non-selectively blocks residual cation and anion crossovers. This mechanism enables an FeF2||NaxSn full cell to achieve a Coulombic efficiency of 99.93% over 200 cycles. Additionally, the S/C||NaxSn system supports extreme rate capabilities (630 mAh g-1 at 20C) and transitions to practical pouch cell configurations, yielding an excellent capacity retention of 91.95% after 1000 cycles at 0.5C. Ultimately, Na-rich nanoalloy anodes offer a compelling pathway toward high-energy, sustainable batteries by transforming electrode crosstalk into a spatiotemporally synergistic anode-cathode coupling.

title: High-Entropy Complementary d-Band Decoupling of Redox Kinetics for Bidirectional Catalysis in Lithium-Sulfur Batteries.
abstract: NA: The reversible conversion of sulfur and Li2S in lithium-sulfur (Li-S) batteries is limited by the bidirectional redox kinetics. A single-component catalyst is difficult to simultaneously meet the differentiated adsorption and catalytic requirements in the multi-step conversion of polysulfides. We propose a high-entropy complementary d-band center model, extending the classical d-band center theory to multi-metal systems. The complementary d-band centers of multiple metals align the HOMO and LUMO of sulfur species, coordinating the electron transfer balance and accelerating the redox kinetics. The multi-metal sites collaboratively construct a "highly efficient capture → cascade conversion → rapid desorption" closed-loop pathway, with the d-p hybridization network regulating the adsorption energy and effectively suppressing the shuttle effect. Based on this design, the high-entropy selenide catalyst with a customized electronic structure and strong synergy effect has achieved excellent cycle stability and rate performance in Li-S batteries.

title: Structure-Encoded Magnetic Anisotropy in Super-Tough Magnetoelastic Aramid-Silk-Magnetite Fibers.
abstract: NA: Magnetic anisotropy is essential for controlling magnetic responses in soft matter, yet it is conventionally imposed using external magnetic fields. Here, we show that magnetic anisotropy can instead be intrinsically encoded and continuously tuned through hierarchical structural organization, establishing a route by which anisotropic dipolar interactions, rather than conventional shape effects, dominate the magnetic energy landscape. This mechanism is achieved by engineering composite nanofibrils in which magnetite nanoparticles are grown in situ within an aligned aramid-silk matrix, inspired by biomineralization in chiton teeth. The resulting aramid-silk-magnetite fibers combine high strength and modulus with exceptional toughness up to 820 MJ m- 3, while exhibiting tunable magnetic anisotropy spanning axial to radial easy-axis configurations through structural relaxation. Quantitative analysis reveals that collective dipolar coupling dominates magnetic anisotropy by orders of magnitude over demagnetization-field contributions, identifying nanoparticle interaction networks as the primary origin of anisotropy. This built-in anisotropy enables strain-mediated reconfiguration of magnetic properties, giving rise to magnetoelastic coupling that scales with fiber modulus and reflects the available structural mobility for magnetic reorientation. By amplifying structure-defined anisotropy under mechanical loading, we further demonstrate strain-controlled magnetic torque for actuation. These findings establish a structural design principle for programming magnetic anisotropy in mechanically robust magnetoelastic materials.

title: Unlocking the Potential of Magnesium-Based Hydrogen Storage Composites via Advanced Thermodynamic and Kinetic Tuning Strategies.
abstract: NA: The development of efficient and safe solid-state hydrogen storage technologies is pivotal for the transition toward sustainable clean energy. Magnesium is a promising hydrogen carrier due to its high gravimetric (7.6 wt.% for MgH2) and volumetric storage capacity (110 kg m-3), abundance, and excellent reversibility. However, the practical application of Mg-based materials is hindered by their high thermodynamic stability (ΔH  =    -74.7 kJ mol-1 H2) and sluggish sorption kinetics. Here, we overview the latest advances in Mg-based composites for high hydrogen storage performance. We discuss key material modification strategies, including catalysis, nanostructuring, alloying, and external field assistance to tune the thermodynamic and kinetic properties of Mg-based materials. We stress the emerging role of machine learning in accelerating material design, performance prediction, and optimization. We also critically assess the techno-economic viability of Mg-based hydrogen storage within integrated hydrogen value chains. This assessment considers how storage connects with hydrogen production, transport, and end-use applications. Finally, we outline challenges and future research directions, aiming to guide the rational design of next-generation Mg-based hydrogen storage materials and systems toward commercial applications.

title: Transforming Pathological H2S Into a Photodynamic Amplifier: In Vivo Formation of Bi2O2CO3@Bi2S3 Heterojunction for Microenvironment-Adaptive Periodontitis Treatment.
abstract: NA: Current periodontitis management is hindered by the inability to effectively reverse the dysbiotic microenvironment of persistent infection and restore immune homeostasis. Although photodynamic therapy (PDT) presents a promising non-invasive antibacterial strategy, its clinical efficacy remains limited by poor microenvironmental selectivity and insufficient immunomodulatory capacity. Herein, we engineer a microenvironment-responsive "trash-to-treasure" PDT strategy based on Bi2O2CO3 nanosheet-assembled microspheres. This platform actively scavenges excess hydrogen sulfide (H2S) within the periodontal pocket, triggering an in situ transformation into Bi2O2CO3@Bi2S3 heterojunctions. This H2S-triggered conversion neutralizes the pro-inflammatory gasotransmitter and establishes an S-scheme heterojunction with enhanced photocatalytic activity. The resulting reactive oxygen species (ROS)-mediated oxidative stress, together with targeted disruption of bacterial iron metabolism, enables highly efficient photodynamic eradication of major periodontopathogens such as Porphyromonas gingivalis. Moreover, Bi2O2CO3-mediated scavenging of pathological H2S alleviates inflammatory responses in human gingival fibroblasts and reactivates macrophage respiratory burst for intracellular bacterial clearance. In vivo evaluations in a rat periodontitis model demonstrate effective inflammation resolution, suppression of alveolar bone loss, and robust tissue regeneration. This work introduces an intelligent therapeutic strategy that hijacks pathological H2S as a photodynamic amplifier, establishing a microenvironment-adaptive PDT paradigm for periodontal infection.

title: Nanoscale Thermal Imaging of Dislocation-Mediated Heat Transport.
abstract: NA: Dislocations are widely used to tailor lattice thermal conductivity in semiconductors and thermoelectrics, yet the local thermal resistance of individual buried dislocations and their spatial extent remain experimentally unresolved. Here, operando scanning transmission electron microscopy-electron energy-loss spectroscopy thermometry, atomic-resolution imaging, vibrational spectroscopy, and nonequilibrium molecular dynamics are combined to map heat transport across a dislocation array within a 5°SrTiO3 low-angle grain boundary. The effective thermal conductance of the dislocation array is estimated to be ∼35.4 MW m- 2 K- 1 using the bulk reference conductivity, corresponding to a Kapitza length of ∼339 nm. Nanoscale temperature maps reveal a spatially heterogeneous resistance landscape: reconstructed dislocation cores act as sharp thermal bottlenecks over ∼2.14-5.17 nm, with steeper local temperature gradients than inter-core regions, whereas inter-core regions show weaker but more extended modulation over ∼8.34-11.57 nm. Correlative structural and vibrational analyses show that Ti─O bond distortion, Ti valence change, P4 optical-phonon blueshift, and reduced local-bulk phonon density-of-states overlap create a core-specific vibrational environment. These results uncover the underlying mechanism whereby atomic-scale core reconstruction generates nanoscale localized thermal resistance, and offer quantitative descriptors for defect-structure-guided thermal design.

title: Orthogonal Passivation of Polar Facets for Efficient InSb Quantum Dot SWIR Photodetectors.
abstract: NA: Indium antimonide (InSb) colloidal quantum dots (CQDs) offer a heavy-metal-free route to short-wave infrared (SWIR) photodetection, but their performance still lags behind lead- and mercury-based CQD systems, and the surface chemistry that limits their performance is not well understood. Here, we identify two independent oxide-derived trap pathways on the polar terminations of zincblende InSb: oxidation of the In-terminated {111}A and Sb-terminated {111}B facets creates chemically distinct mid-gap states, each of which degrades carrier transport. Density functional theory calculations show that metal halides bind strongly to Sb-terminated facets, but weakly to In-terminated facets, while thiolates show the opposite preference; this asymmetry leaves single-ligand passivation incomplete. Exploiting this orthogonality, we develop a facet-specific exchange that passivates both terminations and removes their surface oxides in a single step. The resulting CQD films show a fivefold reduction in hole-trap density and a sixfold improvement in hole mobility relative to thiol-only controls. The photodetectors achieve 50% external quantum efficiency under 1 V reverse bias at 1390 nm, to the best of our knowledge, the highest reported for InSb CQD photodetectors in the 1300-1500 nm range, along with a 580 ns fall time and 95% photocurrent retention after 100 h of continuous operation.

title: Planar Focusing of Anisotropic Plasmon Polaritons in MoOCl2/Au.
abstract: NA: Hyperbolic polaritons offer a promising approach for subwavelength light confinement and manipulation. While extensively explored across mid-infrared to terahertz bands, achieving long-distance focusing at visible frequencies remains challenging due to the trade-off between long propagation and strong compression. In this work, we demonstrate planar focusing of anisotropic plasmon polaritons with an extended focal length in a MoOCl2/Au heterostructure. By integrating an Au metastructure with the natural hyperbolic material MoOCl2, we convert surface plasmon polaritons (SPPs) into surface plasmon hyperbolic polaritons (SPHPs), enabling excitation and focusing of the low-momentum hybrid anisotropic polariton in the heterostructure. Furthermore, by optimizing the thickness of the MoOCl2 layer, we synergistically enhance both the propagation distance and the field compression. Using transmission-mode scanning near-field optical microscopy (SNOM) and quantitative methods, we demonstrate a focal length of 2.5λ and a focal spot with a full width at half maximum (FWHM) of λ/5 under 633 nm excitation, accompanied by a threefold energy enhancement. This visible-frequency long-focus system offers significant potential for noncontact nanoscale probing, integrated photonics, and optical interconnects. The proposed heterostructure engineering approach provides a versatile design paradigm for coupling hyperbolic polaritons with multiple plasmonic excitations, paving the way for advanced photonic applications.

title: Engineering Topological Phases in Two-Dimensional Materials: A Path from Preparation to Device Applications.
abstract: NA: Owing to their topologically protected edge or surface states, rapid electronic transport, and highly tunable physical properties, two-dimensional topological materials (2D TMs) have garnered significant attention in condensed matter physics and materials science, and are regarded as potential candidates for quantum computing. Since the first observation of the quantum Hall effect, fundamental research on the physics of TMs has made remarkable progress. To better utilize the unique properties of TMs, the importance of material fabrication and phase engineering of topological states has become increasingly prominent. This review systematically discusses phase engineering in 2D TMs, from their growth to device applications. First, various topological phases and related 2D materials are introduced briefly. Next, the growth methods for 2D TMs are summarized. It then discusses progress and limitations in growth, driven by the requirements of characterization and application. Furthermore, the general approaches for modulating topological phases are reviewed, alongside the current applications in electronic devices. Finally, the review outlines future directions and challenges in phase engineering of 2D topological materials, aiming to promote the transition of 2D TMs from fundamental physics research to phase-engineered material platforms.

title: Hydro-Gated Photonic Actuators With Programmable Color and Shape.
abstract: NA: Structural color actuators integrating visual readout with motion are prized for biomimicry, yet typically operate in a coupled, color-gradient mode with limited freedom. Here we report a photonic liquid crystal network that decouples these responses via a scattering-gated mechanism. The material hides its structural color in the dry state but, upon water uptake, simultaneously switches on vivid coloration and executes programmable three-dimensional deformation. Crucially, we achieve stimulus-selective control: ethanol turns on color without motion, while heat induces motion without color. This independent, on-demand manipulation of optical and mechanical outputs offers a transformative platform for multi-responsive soft robotics, adaptive camouflage, and smart displays.

title: Over 95% Optical Reflectance From Structurally Modulated All-Biopolymer Multilayers.
abstract: NA: Sustainable photonics aims to replace conventional optical materials with environmentally benign alternatives, yet its development is fundamentally constrained by the narrow intrinsic refractive-index variability of biopolymers. Here we show that a dense-porous periodic architecture yields nearly perfect optical reflection using only polysaccharides. By exploiting the difference in skeletal rigidity between amorphous pectin and crystalline cellulose nanofibers (CNFs), we form alternating dense, high-refractive-index pectin layers and porous, low-refractive-index CNF layers through a combination of electrodeposition with solvent exchange. This dense-porous periodic architecture yields reflectivities exceeding 97% in the visible range and 95% in the near-infrared-a range unprecedented for biopolymer-based optical materials. Moreover, the strategy is simple, scalable, and highly versatile, enabling free spectral design across the visible and near-infrared regions, broadband metallic-like reflection, and planar patterning within a single fabrication process. Combined with the low thermal conductivity arising from porous layers and the coexistence of visible transparency and near-infrared reflection, the resulting films show potential as transparent thermal-management materials. This work establishes a new materials design principle for biodegradable, polysaccharide-based photonic systems and advances the field of sustainable photonics.

title: Ultra-Long Helical CNFs 3D-Networks as High-Conductivity Current Collectors for Efficient Sodium Deposition.
abstract: NA: Aluminum (Al) current collectors are crucial for sodium metal batteries (SMBs), yet sodium (Na) dendrite suppression and uniform Na deposition remain challenges. Surface modification could significantly optimize Na deposition behavior. Herein, a 20 nm copper (Cu) layer is designed to confine NiY diatomic catalyst (DAC) for Al surface modification via magnetron sputtering and heat treatment. The adjacent NiY atoms, with low single-point energy (-228.05 eV), minimum segregation energy (-0.67 eV), and maximum aggregation energy (5.84 eV), synergistically stabilize diatomic dispersion in the Cu nanolayer. Benefiting from the tailored acetylene adsorption energy (-1.16 eV) and favorable formation energies of C2H (-13.58 eV) and C2 (-11.44 eV), NiY-DAC exhibits excellent catalytic activity, in-situ growth ultra-long helical CNFs 3D-networks with a thickness of 46.3 µm on Al current collectors, enabling efficient Na storage and remarkable inhibition Na dendrite formation. The modified current collector delivers outstanding electrochemical performance. The coulombic efficiency is up to 99.49% over 3000 h of half-cells at 1.0 mA cm-2/1.0 mAh cm-2 with a low overpotential (3.1 mV), and the CNFs-Na||Na3V2(PO4)3 full-cells achieve stable cycling over 1500 cycles at 10.0 C. This diatomic catalyst confinement strategy provides new insight into designing high-performance carbon-modified current collectors.

title: Flexible High-Speed Low-Noise Organic Photodiode Arrays for Dynamic Near-Infrared Imaging.
abstract: NA: Organic photodiodes (OPDs) hold significant promise for next-generation IoT optical sensing and low-power imaging applications. However, widespread application of OPD in flexible and dynamic imaging has been constrained by high dark current, poor stability, and the lack of a cost-effective imaging system. In this work, we present an integrated solution through tailoring pseudo-planar heterojunction (PPHJ) OPD arrays and a customized, rapidly accessible imaging system, the dynamic organic photonics imaging system (DOIS). The resulting PPHJ OPD exhibited a high responsivity (0.6 A W-1 at 868 nm), low dark current (1.5 × 10-8 A cm-2 at -1 V) and fast response time (480 ns), benefiting from optimal vertical phase separation and donor-acceptor interface morphology. Moreover, flexible photodetector exhibits superior mechanical stability, photostability and storage stability. Crucially, a pixel-shifting strategy was incorporated into conventional convolutional neural network (CNN) based machine learning algorithms to capture dynamic images and enhance resolution by leveraging sub-pixel information sampling. This work demonstrates a significant potential for the extensive application of organic photovoltaic materials in image sensing and flexible electronics.

title: Crystallinity-Governed Liquid Wettability and Mobility on Solid Surface.
abstract: NA: Control over liquid wettability and droplet mobility is essential for several emerging applications including open microfluidics, anti-icing, self-cleaning, and heat transfer. Existing strategies generally rely on permanent chemical modification or continuous external stimuli to regulate droplet spreading, pinning, and sliding. Here, we report a unified approach for reconfiguring wettability states and droplet mobility by regulating crystalline packing of a semicrystalline polymer. A phase-transitioning polymer, poly(octadecyl acrylate) (PODAc), was incorporated into a porous polymeric coating, where melting and subsequent cooling pathways determine the extent of alkyl-chain crystallization and interfacial polar functionality. Cooling in air or underwater generates reversibly switchable hydrophilic (θW ∼ 85°), hydrophobic (θW ∼ 104°), and amphiphobic slippery states across liquids with surface tensions of 22-72 mN m-1. These distinct regimes enable programmable droplet spreading, pinning, and low-friction transport without post-synthetic chemical treatment or sustained external stimulation. Furthermore, reconfigurable wettability patterns enable guided liquid transport through spatially selective complete wetting or customized contact line frictional force.

title: Additives and Relaxation Fluidize Molecular Transport Within Covalent Adaptable Networks.
abstract: NA: Incorporating dynamic covalent bonds into polymer networks could offer stimuli-responsive control over molecular transport, often requiring additives to facilitate bond rearrangement. Here super-resolution localization microscopy was employed to examine fluorescent probe transport in unhydrated, elastic networks containing thiol-thioester dynamic covalent chemistry (DCC). In static, DCC-free networks, displacement distributions revealed frequent trapping and slow, anomalous, and heterogeneous diffusion. Introducing a dynamic catalyst additive markedly increased mobile fraction and produced diffusivity that was more fluid-like. These effects were observed with several classes of fluorescent probes, two distinct additives, and for networks with or without DCC. Experiments with a photo-releasable catalyst (NPPOC-TMG) separated additive effects from those of activated exchange. Catalyst release conferred additional fluidization of the network. Importantly, these changes were not accompanied by macroscopic plasticization, suggesting that small additive concentrations can strongly affect transport in confining environments. Spatial analysis further indicated that transport enhancement was primarily due to restructuring of an initially heterogeneous network rather than local bond exchange near the diffusing probes. Additive incorporation and post-cure exchange likely reduced defects and homogenized the crosslink density. In sum, these results demonstrate how DCC modulates transport, emphasize the importance of the activation method, and highlight its potential in separation and controlled-release systems.

title: Ultra-Broad-Temperature Mechanoluminescence Enabled by Intrinsic Lattice Disorder.
abstract: NA: Mechanoluminescent (ML) materials convert mechanical stimuli into light through carrier excitation and radiative recombination, enabling external-power-free stress sensing and visualization. The strict energy matching required for carrier release, transport, and recombination restricts ML to narrow thermal windows. Their application at extreme temperatures, however, is constrained by discrete defect levels arising from relatively uniform local atomic environments. Here, we use intrinsic lattice disorder to engineer a quasi-continuous trap landscape in Sr3Gd2(Ge3O9)2:Mn2+. Diverse local crystal-field environments, together with dynamically generated defects, create energetically adjacent traps that support a trap-relay process. Charge carriers are continuously redistributed across this trap manifold, sustaining stable ML over an ultrabroad temperature range from 133 to 433 K. We further demonstrate a human-machine interaction system based on this material under simulated extreme-temperature conditions. These results establish intrinsic lattice disorder as a strategy for broadening the thermal operating window of ML materials and provide a general design principle for thermally robust, energy-storing luminescent materials for extreme environments.

title: Scalable Gigapascal Strength Bamboo Veneers via Nanocellulose Reinforcement.
abstract: NA: Carbon neutrality demands materials that deliver both performance and low environmental impact. Carbon fiber and glass fiber rely on fossil feedstocks and energy-intensive processing, while nature bamboo the ecological marvel is limited by inefficient load transfer within their heterogeneous cell walls. Here we show that this limitation can be overcome by reprogramming the bamboo cell wall through supramolecular nano-reinforcement. Cellulose nanocrystals infiltrate the cell wall and promote the reorganization of the interfacial hydrogen-bonding network within the aligned cellulose framework converting structural discontinuities into a continuous load-bearing scaffold. This enhances interfibrillar stress transfer and homogenizes mechanical response across scales. The resulting material achieves a tensile strength of 0.98 GPa and a Young's modulus of 52.7 GPa, with specific strength rivaling many synthetic fiber materials. These gains are achieved with up to two orders of magnitude lower carbon intensity than that of carbon fiber. This work demonstrates a scalable route to transform abundant biomass into high-performance structural materials, decoupling mechanical performance from carbon intensity.

title: PASS-Derived O/S Donor Field-Directed Competitive-Cooperative Fe/Co Phase Evolution for Cross-Band Microwave Absorption.
abstract: NA: Fe/Co bimetallic regulation enables high-performance microwave absorbers, yet the role of intrinsic coordination disparity in precursor conversion, nonequilibrium phase evolution, and cross-band loss redistribution remains unclear. We design a poly(arylene sulfide sulfone) (PASS)-predefined O/S heterogeneous donor-field strategy to direct competitive-cooperative nonequilibrium phase evolution in Fe/Co systems. Covalently embedded sulfone-O and thioether-S sites, with PASS's rigid backbone, create a molecularly preorganized donor field that amplifies non-equivalent Fe/Co coordination, promoting competitive bonding, differentiated phase pathways, and electronic-state reconstruction during confined pyrolysis. Fe/Co regulation thus reshapes local phases, O/S chemical environments, and interfacial charge states via Fe─O/Co─S coordination preferences, generating multiphase heterostructures, amorphous/crystalline interfaces, defects, and lattice strain while balancing dielectric polarization, conductive transport, magnetic response, and impedance matching. The resulting CFC absorber achieves cross-band absorption in low-frequency 5G and high-frequency radar bands. CFC-4 exhibits -73.83 dB at 6.23 GHz (3.20 mm) and -76.59 dB at 16.98 GHz (1.31 mm), with a maximum EAB of 5.03 GHz. CFC-4∼6 (1-5 mm) show >90% cumulative effective absorption over 2-18 GHz. Finite-element simulations reveal a maximum RCS reduction of 42.5 dB on PEC. This work establishes O/S donor-field engineering as a viable route to amplify Fe/Co coordination differentiation for efficient cross-band microwave absorption.

title: Sulfur Locking and Chlorination Synergistically Enable Efficient Charge Transport and Low Nonradiative Energy Loss in Organic Solar Cells.
abstract: NA: Achieving efficient charge transport while maintaining low nonradiative energy loss remains a key challenge in the molecular design of small-molecule acceptors (SMAs) for organic solar cells (OSCs). Herein, we report a stepwise molecular engineering strategy based on sulfur locking and chlorination to regulate intermolecular packing and excited-state properties simultaneously. Sulfur locking modifies molecular conformation and intermolecular packing, leading to enhanced exciton diffusion and charge transport. Subsequent chlorination further strengthens intermolecular interactions through additional Cl···S contacts, resulting in tighter π-π stacking and improved crystalline ordering. Binary OSCs based on D18:Qx2Ph-SCl achieve an efficiency of 20.0% with a high open-circuit voltage (VOC) of 0.951 V, while maintaining a low nonradiative energy loss of ∼0.19 eV. Owing to its intrinsically lower reorganization energy and weaker electron-phonon coupling than L8-BO, Qx2Ph-SCl further serves as an effective third component in ternary OSCs, reducing nonradiative recombination and increasing the VOC. As a result, the ternary device delivers an efficiency of 21.3%. This work demonstrates that stepwise sulfur locking and chlorination provide an effective molecular design strategy for simultaneously optimizing charge transport and voltage loss in high-performance OSCs.

title: Lignin-Based Supramolecular Dynamic Networks: A General Platform for Energy Harvesting and Sensing.
abstract: NA: Lignin- based ionogels are promising sustainable materials for flexible electronics, yet their development is limited by a persistent tradeoff between mechanical robustness and dynamic multifunctionality. Here, we report a rigid flexible supramolecular design strategy that transforms lignin from a rigid bio-based component into an active network building block for dynamic ionogels. By coupling rigid lignin derived domains with flexible dynamic polymer segments, the resulting ionogel achieves efficient energy dissipation, reversible network reconstruction, and stable ionic transport. The ionogel exhibits an elongation at break of 1564%, underwater adhesion strength of 488.3 kPa on steel, and near complete self-healing at room temperature. It further functions as a strain sensor with a gauge factor of 2.83 and stable signal output over 350 stretching cycles. When assembled into a triboelectric nanogenerator, the ionogel delivers a stable voltage output of 75 V under deformation. This work establishes a lignin derived dynamic ionogel platform that integrates robustness, adaptability, sensing, and mechanical energy harvesting for sustainable flexible electronics.

title: Selective Hydrogen Transport Through Polymeric Fullerene Nanosheet Membranes.
abstract: NA: Lamellar membranes, assembled from two-dimensional (2D) nanosheets, have attracted intensive attention for molecular and ion sieving due to their tunable interlayer channels and ultrathin selective layers. However, molecular transport in conventional lamellar membranes usually occurs through interlayer galleries whose dimensions vary with stacking, limiting ångström-scale control over selectivity. Therefore, developing a novel lamellar membrane with ångström-scale in-plane pores is highly desirable. In an idealized qTP lattice, four-directionally connected fullerene cages define periodically distributed apertures that converge from an approximately 5.87 Å entrance to a 3.11 Å waist. Upon assembly, the constriction regions can discriminate by size, while their converging entrances and the intersheet galleries govern molecular access and transport resistance through the in-plane apertures. The resulting polymeric fullerene nanosheet membrane exhibits an H2 permeance of 3896 ± 107 GPU and an H2/CO2 separation factor of 88.5 ± 5.9 for the separation of an equimolar H2/CO2 mixture at 303.15 K and a total feed pressure of 100 kPa. The separation performance remains stable over 200 h of operation. This study establishes topology-encoded pore geometry as a design principle for integrating short selective pathways with ångström-scale molecular discrimination in lamellar membranes.

title: Dichlorobenzodithiophene-4-8-dione Derived Polymer Donor Enables Efficient Thin-Film/Thick-Film Organic Solar Cells.
abstract: NA: Polymer donors with electron-withdrawing benzodithiophene-4-8-dione (BDD) unit play an important role in improving power-conversion-efficiency (PCE) of organic solar cells (OSCs), although these achievements rely on high-cost electron-donating fluorinated thienyl-benzodithiophene (BDTT) moiety. Herein, a dichlorobenzodithiophene-4-8-dione (BDD2Cl) unit is developed to design fluorine-free BDTT-alt-BDD2Cl-structured cost-effective polymer donor (PBDTT-BDD2Cl). Compared to its halogen-free BDTT-alt-BDD-structured control (PBDB-T), PBDTT-BDD2Cl shows deep-shifted energy levels, improved solubility, crystallinity, and packing, tending to suppress energy loss, manipulate film-forming kinetics, and improve charge transport properties. Accordingly, the PBDTT-BDD2Cl:L8-BO device demonstrates dramatically higher photovoltage (0.947 V) and lower non-radiative energy loss (0.182 eV) and compared to the PBDB-T:L8-BO device (0.735 and 0.369 eV), while it achieves decreased PCE. When incorporating it into D18:L8-BO host, ternary D18:PBDTT-BDD2Cl:L8-BO shows optimized donor/acceptor miscibility, delayed material nucleation, and prolonged molecular ordered packing duration, leading to boosted charge dynamics and favorable morphology. Thereby, thin-film (100 nm) OSC achieves a superior PCE (21.1%, certified as 20.6%, ranking among the highest values) than the D18:PBDB-T:L8-BO control (19.3%), while its thick-film (500 nm) device also obtains a top-high PCE (17.3%) among these reported thick-films (≥500 nm). This work highlights that BDD2Cl is an ideal candidate for developing cost-effective polymer donors toward efficient thin-film/thick-film OSCs.

title: High-Mobility p-Type TexSe1- x Films With Yb-Enabled Oxidation Suppression for Short-Wave Infrared Imaging Detection.
abstract: NA: Scalable high-mobility p-type semiconductor films hold considerable promise for advancing the performance of both photoelectronic devices and complementary metal-oxide-semiconductor technologies. Currently, tellurium (Te)-based semiconductors exhibit high intrinsic hole mobility and compatibility with low-temperature processing, making them promising candidates for cost-effective p-type materials. However, owing to their low Gibbs free energy, they are prone to oxidation into TeO2, which introduces deep-level defects and severely degrades hole transport, thereby hindering practical applications. Here, we present an effective antioxidant strategy based on ytterbium (Yb) doping, wherein the strong Te-Yb bonding and high oxygen affinity of Yb effectively suppress the oxidation of Te to TeO2, fundamentally stabilizing TexSe1- x alloys. The resulting Te0.7Se0.3:Yb films exhibit a remarkable hole mobility of 177.5 cm2 V-1 s-1. Furthermore, ZnO/Te0.7Se0.3:Yb photodetectors achieve a high responsivity of 0.21 A/W at 1300 nm, enabling multispectral imaging for precise target discrimination. These results demonstrate the Yb-enabled oxidation suppression for Te-based semiconductor, making a crucial stride toward the establishment of commercially viable high-mobility p-type semiconductor technology and short-wavelength infrared photoelectronics.

title: Homojunction Back Contacts Enable Efficient Cu2O Photocathodes.
abstract: NA: Enhancing carrier separation and extraction is crucial to achieve efficient metal oxide photoelectrodes for photoelectrochemical (PEC) water splitting. Here, we report a highly efficient Cu2O photocathode based on p+/p back-contact homojunction. The homojunction significantly enhances hole-selective extraction while suppressing electron backflow at the back-contact interface, leading to marked improvements in PEC performance. The optimized photocathode delivers a hydrogen evolution reaction (HER) onset potential of 1.1 V and a saturated photocurrent density of ∼8.0 mA cm-2. Furthermore, the p+/p back homojunction design enables the fabrication of a semi-transparent Cu2O photocathode, which, when integrated with a perovskite solar cell in a tandem configuration, achieves a solar-to-hydrogen (STH) efficiency of 7.31%. This work demonstrates a viable strategy for advancing metal oxide photoelectrodes via homojunction engineering.

title: Cross-System Recycling of Spent Layered Oxides Boosts Synergistic Optimization of Na4Fe3(PO4)2P2O7 Cathodes via Site-Selective Ni/Mn Co-Doping.
abstract: NA: To address the economic inviability of recycling spent sodium-ion batteries (SIBs) and the intrinsic drawbacks of Na4Fe3(PO4)2P2O7 (NFPP) cathodes, a "cross-system recycling" strategy is proposed to transform the waste layered oxides cathodes (NaNi1/3Fe1/3Mn1/3O2, NFM) into high-performance polyanionic cathodes (Na4Fe2.9Ni0.05Mn0.05(PO4)2P2O7, NFNMPP). Nickel and manganese in the waste NFM that degrades due to "sodium deficiency" and irreversible phase transitions are leached out and doped into the NFNMPP lattice. Benefiting from the synergistic optimization of NFNMPP via site-selective Ni/Mn co-doping, the impurities and [P2O7] distortion are suppressed, while the conductivity and Na+ diffusion kinetics are enhanced. Consequently, the high-purity NFNMPP (91.2%) exhibits an ideal initial coulombic efficiency of 92.84%, remarkable rate capability (75.21 mAh g-1 at 50 C), and excellent cycling stability (86.74% capacity retention after 12 000 cycles at 20 C). Furthermore, paired with hard carbon (HC) anode, NFNMPP//HC pouch cells exhibit high safety, a record-long cycling life of 5557 cycles, 82.37% capacity retention at 30 C, and a wide operating temperature range (-40°C to 55°C), demonstrating great potential for energy storage applications and powering low-speed electric vehicles. This study presents a viable pathway for optimizing cathode materials by recycling spent SIBs, and facilitates its practical applications validated by Ah-level pouch cells.

title: Attribution Fingerprinting by Interpretable Machine Learning Reveals Category-Specific Additive Design Rules for Zinc Anodes.
abstract: NA: Electrolyte additives are one of the most direct remedy for interfacial instability in aqueous zinc-ion batteries, yet their development remains empirical. Existing machine-learning (ML) screening strategies presume a single global structure-property relationship shared by all additives. Here, an interpretable ML framework predicts cycle life from molecular descriptors and test conditions, and molecule-specific SHapley Additive exPlanations (SHAP) profiles serve as attribution fingerprints. Unsupervised clustering resolves the additives into three attribution-based categories, governed respectively by adsorption energetics, charge-transfer gap and hydrogen-bond-network regulation, indicating that one universal descriptor set may not hold across chemically distinct additives. Representative additives from each category, none present in the training set, agree with experiment to within 11%. Category I screening identifies 2-fluoropyridine-5-carbaldehyde (2FPD), predicted at 3218 h, and Zn//Zn cells deliver 3010 h at 1 mA cm-2 and 1 mAh cm-2, within 6.5% of prediction. Structural controls trace the improvement to the aldehyde: retaining it alone gives 900 h against an 89 h baseline, whereas fluorine alone gives 90 h. 2FPD constructs a graded organic-inorganic interphase that limits water access to the zinc surface and accelerates Zn2+ desolvation, and Zn//MnO2 full cells retain 96% capacity over 4000 cycles. This workflow offers a route towards interpretability-guided additive design.

title: Quasi-Continuous Multimodal Sensing of Urinary Oxalate Dynamics for Home-Based Metabolic Monitoring.
abstract: NA: Continuous at-home monitoring of urinary oxalate dynamics is vital for the comprehensive management of hyperoxaluria and thus reduces the risk of kidney stone formation. However, home-based devices for capturing dynamic oxalate profiles remain elusive, as urine is challenging to sample and unstable for subsequent biochemical testing. Here we report a remote multimodal sensing platform for achieving such urine monitoring during daily sequential urination through seamless embedding into a standard urine collection bucket. This platform integrates electrochemical oxalate sensing with simultaneous pH and urine-volume measurements to correct the matrix drift in oxalate quantification. We achieve quasi-continuous monitoring of 24 h urinary physicochemical dynamics under diet-induced transient hyperoxaluria. By decoupling oxalate concentration from multimodal signals per urination, we reveal distinct metabolic response profiles under different dietary oxalate loads, providing new real-time insights into oxalate metabolism and its associated risk of kidney stones. Our all-in-one sampling-and-testing platform could revolutionize clinical urine analysis for hyperoxaluria, shifting from a one-time, multi-day turnaround assay into a paradigm of quasi-continuous monitoring with immediate feedback. This work represents a practical route toward personalized management of hyperoxaluria and a decentralized metabolic monitoring strategy for urology.

title: A Retinal Matrix Stiffening Model Reveals FAK-Dependent Mechanotransduction in Pericytes Underlies Vascular Destabilization.
abstract: NA: Pericyte loss, an early hallmark of diabetic retinopathy (DR), is linked to hyperglycemia and inflammation, whereas the contribution of mechanical changes in the retina remains unclear. We define design parameters for an iPSC-derived microphysiological system (MPS) comprising pericyte-endothelial capillary networks embedded in a dynamically stiffening hydrogel engineered to reproduce matrix stiffening in a controlled, human-relevant context. Microrheology of Ins2Akita mouse retinas revealed increased storage modulus in perivascular regions at a diabetic timepoint coincident with reduced pericyte coverage and vascular remodeling, establishing a stiffness magnitude used to inform the design of the MPS. In the MPS, progressive matrix stiffening alone, in the absence of hyperglycemic exposure, was sufficient to induce analogous vascular defects and to suppress pericyte expression of NOTCH3, HEY1, JAG1, and N-cadherin in a focal adhesion kinase (FAK)-dependent manner. Inhibition of FAK restored pericyte signaling and vascular integrity in stiffened conditions without altering soft controls, identifying a FAK-dependent mechanotransduction as a druggable target. Single-cell RNA-sequencing of human diabetic retinas validated enrichment of focal-adhesion components and alterations in Notch-pathway transcripts in pericytes. These findings establish a human MPS showing matrix stiffening as a key regulator of pericyte-mediated vascular stabilization and nominate it and FAK-dependent mechanotransduction as targets to prevent DR pathogenesis.

title: Sub-10 nm Confined Channels in Edge-Closed MXene Nanoribbons Boost Proton Transport for Efficient Single-Atom Electrocatalysts.
abstract: NA: Nanoribbons from atomic layers such as graphene, carbides, and nitrides (MXenes) have attracted considerable interest owing to their distinct quantum confinement effects and high surface activity. However, the controlled synthesis of MXene nanoribbons remains challenging due to their random fragmentation and poor stability. Here, an efficient stiffness-mediated strategy is developed to fabricate unique edge-closed MXene nanoribbons, featuring a large aspect ratio of 10∼40 and confined channels of sub-10 nm at both edges. The key protocol involves modulating the critical collapse pressure by reducing the bending stiffness of MXene layers, thereby triggering the tube collapse of pre-formed nanoscrolls into edge-closed nanoribbons upon solvent evaporation. The resulting nanoribbons exhibit an enhanced polarization electric field, leading to a higher surface proton concentration and enhanced proton transport rate compared to nanoscrolls and nanosheets. As a result, these MXene nanoribbons provide an efficient platform for anchoring single-atom Pt, achieving a low overpotential of 23 mV at 10 mA cm-2 and a Tafel slope of 25 mV dec-1 in the hydrogen evolution reaction (HER), outperforming the most reported electrocatalysts.

title: Anchored Fluoro-Shielded Solvation for Lithium Metal Batteries.
abstract: NA: Polyvinylidene fluoride (PVDF)-based polymer electrolytes are promising candidates for solid-state lithium metal batteries owing to their favorable overall electrochemical properties. However, conventional PVDF-based polymer electrolytes suffer from uneven solvation distribution, discontinuous ion-transport pathways, and unstable electrode/electrolyte interfaces caused by residual solvents and porous PVDF frameworks. Herein, we report an anchored fluoro-shielded solvation strategy to construct a high-performance PVDF-based polymer electrolyte. By integrating polyanionic anchoring sites with fluorinated shielding segments, the optimized electrolyte enables spatially distributed anion-rich solvation pathways, homogeneous Li+ transport, and robust LiF-rich solid electrolyte interphase (SEI). The polymer electrolyte delivers a high ionic conductivity of 1.26×10-3 S cm-1, a Li+ transference number of 0.69, an oxidative onset potential of 5.27 V, and a critical current density of 6.4 mA cm-2. Spectroscopic and interfacial analyses reveal that the anchored fluoro-shielded solvation structure promotes LiF-rich SEI formation and suppresses solvent decomposition. Consequently, Li||LiNi0.8Co0.1Mn0.1O2 batteries retain 80.2% capacity after 2000 cycles under high-voltage and high-rate conditions of 4.5 V and 5 C. This work highlights anchored fluoro-shielded solvation as an effective molecular design principle for advanced polymer electrolytes toward practical high-voltage and high-rate solid-state Li metal batteries.

title: Suprasilica Nanosieves for Selective Capture of Aromatics Over Cyclic Aliphatics in Hydrocarbon Feedstocks.
abstract: NA: Separating aromatic from cyclic aliphatic hydrocarbons remains a major challenge, as conventional distillation is both energy-intensive and poorly selective. Here, we report supramolecular silica nanosieves (suprasilica) that integrate organic molecular recognition sites directly into robust inorganic matrices. A hexasila-ureido-trianglamine (Δ-Si6) is co-condensed within the silica matrix through a self-assembly sol-gel approach at controlled loadings to produce suprasilica sieves (Δ-SiNx). In vapor sorption, Δ-SiNx reject cyclic aliphatic hydrocarbons while displaying high aromatic uptake, achieving benchmark ideal selectivity for benzene over cyclohexane (23.5, uptake 9.4 mmol g- 1) on Δ-SiN20 and for toluene over methylcyclohexane (6.3, uptake 6.3 mmol g- 1) on Δ-SiN10. The selectivity was further confirmed by Dynamic Column Breakthrough experiments, which demonstrated efficient separation under dynamic conditions. Importantly, the Δ-SiNx retain their molecular discrimination in the binary liquid phase, showing strong preferential uptake while preserving aromatic selectivity in neat naphtha and in diluted crude oil. Metadynamics simulations indicate that the selectivity is kinetic in origin, benzene passing the macrocyclic apertures with a modest barrier while cyclohexane is excluded. These suprasilica nanosieves deliver benchmark separation performance and provide a scalable, energy-efficient strategy for hydrocarbon purification.

title: Dead Cell-Based Carriers: Strategies, Biomedical Applications, and Prospects.
abstract: NA: Living cells have been explored for drug delivery due to their active motility and homing ability; however, their potential toxicity, uncontrolled proliferation, and poor stability severely hinder their practical application and clinical translation. In recent years, dead cells have emerged as promising delivery vehicles due to their enhanced safety, improved stability, and retention of key bioactive molecules. In this review, we summarize the fabrication strategies and delivery characteristics of four types of dead carriers including microalgae, yeasts, bacteria, and mammalian cells in treating diseases such as bacterial pneumonia, inflammatory bowel disease, and cancer. We also discuss the therapeutic mechanisms of endogenous bioactive components, platform-specific limitations, and the advantages/disadvantages of dead cell-based carriers. Finally, we formulate general design principles for dead cell carriers and provide a forward-looking perspective on key translational bottlenecks, including safety assessment, standardized manufacturing, and regulatory pathways, with the aim of guiding the development of safe and effective dead cell-based delivery systems.

title: Synchronous and Unidirectional Epitaxy of Layer-Controlled Graphene on Oxidized Single-Crystal Copper Wafers With Tunable Stacking Order.
abstract: NA: The deterministic synthesis of wafer-scale two-dimensional (2D) materials with programmable layer number, crystallographic orientation, and stacking order is essential for unlocking their layer-dependent quantum properties and enabling scalable device integration. Here, we demonstrate a synchronous and unidirectional epitaxy strategy for chemical vapor deposition growth of layer-controlled graphene on atomically flat oxidized single-crystal Cu wafers. Using a Cu(111)-Cu2O(111) heterogeneous catalytic substrate, we achieved 2-inch single-crystalline graphene films with precisely tunable layer numbers (2 to 5). By engineering the atomic steps of high-index Cu surfaces, we created deterministic spatial patterning of alternating Bernal and rhombohedral stacking in trilayer graphene, as confirmed by near-field nano-optics and angle-resolved photoemission spectroscopy. The resulting wafer-scale films exhibit exceptional thickness uniformity, high crystallinity, and an ultra-flat surface. This work provides a unified growth framework that concurrently resolves the intertwined challenges of layer control, wafer-scale single crystallinity, and stacking order modulation, laying a material foundation for advanced device studies and potential applications.

title: Underlying Mechanisms of Helicobacter pylori in Caries Progression and the Corresponding Dual-Responsive Hydrogel-Based Intervention.
abstract: NA: Helicobacter pylori (H. pylori) infects nearly half of the global population. Given that H. pylori is considered poorly adapted to the oral environment, previous studies have mainly focused on gastric infection. By contrast, how H. pylori persists in the oral cavity and relates to oral diseases remains unclear. This study investigates the role of H. pylori in caries progression. The results show that H. pylori is retained within Streptococcus mutans (S. mutans) biofilms, and its presence is associated with transcriptional remodeling in S. mutans, alongside increased overall cariogenic potential of the mixed biofilm. In a rat caries model, H. pylori co-colonization aggravates caries progression and oral microbiota dysbiosis. To address this pathological niche, a multifunctional hydrogel, termed GPAM, is designed by integrating a Cu2O@Pt heterojunction (MCP) with amorphous calcium phosphate (ACP). Under activation by yellow light and ultrasound, MCP generates reactive oxygen species (ROS) to disrupt S. mutans-H. pylori mixed biofilms. Meanwhile, released Cu2+ reduces H. pylori urease activity, and ACP promotes tooth remineralization. GPAM also shows microbiota-modulating potential. Together, these findings provide insight into H. pylori-associated caries progression and support GPAM as a multifunctional therapeutic strategy for mixed biofilms and caries-related damage.

title: Re(I)-Based Molecular Actuator-Equipped Nanomotors for Integrated Photodynamic and Photomechanical Therapy of Solid Tumor.
abstract: NA: The dense stromal barrier of solid tumors severely hinders intratumoral distribution and therapeutic performance of conventional nanomedicines, and such limitation further compromises oxygen-dependent photodynamic therapy. Herein, through molecular engineering, we develop a Janus nanomotor (Re1@NMs) that integrates a three-dimensional rhenium(I)-based molecular actuator (Re1) with glucose oxidase (GOx)-powered propulsion. Owing to the Janus structure, asymmetric GOx-catalyzed glucose consumption generates local chemical gradients that fuel autonomous motility, thereby enhancing intratumoral distribution. Upon light activation, the engineered Re1, screened from six Re(I) complexes, functions both as a dual Type I/II photosensitizer generating reactive oxygen species (ROS) to induce oxidative stress and as a molecular actuator whose Y-axis motif undergoes E/Z photoisomerization and torsional deformation, thereby contributing to membrane permeabilization. The resulting integrated mechano-photodynamic action coordinately activates ferroptosis and pyroptosis. In a murine tumor model, Re1@NMs-mediated phototherapy achieves superior tumor suppression with excellent biosafety and further elicits robust antitumor immunity, as evidenced by enhanced dendritic cell maturation, increased tumor-infiltrating T cells, elevated effector cytokine expression, and damage-associated molecular pattern release. To the best of our knowledge, this work represents the first integration of a deliberately engineered metal-complex-based three-dimensional molecular actuator with a tumor-microenvironment-adaptive nanomotor, establishing a new paradigm for overcoming tumor barriers.

title: Chemically Reactivatable Sulfide Interfaces for Low-Pressure Thick-Cathode Solid-State Na-S Batteries.
abstract: NA: Low-pressure solid-state Na-S batteries with thick sulfur cathodes are attractive for high-energy storage, but their operation is fundamentally constrained by the progressive loss of solid-solid contact during sulfur conversion. Once insulating sulfides become poorly connected to the electronic network, charge recovery becomes incomplete and cathode passivation rapidly accumulates. Here, we construct chemically reactivatable sulfide interfaces by embedding Fe3C-MnO heteropoints within nitrogen-doped hollow carbon nanotubes. The heterointerface integrates carbon-side electronic coupling, sulfide-side affinity, and interfacial polarization, thereby suppressing localized sulfide accumulation and sustaining charge-stage sulfur recovery as mechanical confinement weakens. This effect is strongly pressure dependent. Under high compression, the electrochemical responses of different hosts converge, whereas under contact-limited conditions the Fe3C-MnO architecture preserves markedly higher sulfur utilization, lower polarization, and superior cycling stability. Consequently, the operational pressure required to retain ≥80% of the 10 MPa discharge capacity decreases from approximately 2 MPa for the control cathodes to 0.2 MPa for Fe3C-MnO/NC@S. A 200 µm cathode with 8.3 mg cm-2 sulfur sustains reversible cycling at 0.2 MPa, together with a pouch-cell energy density of 696 Wh kgcathode -1. These results establish sulfide-interface reactivation as a route to decouple reversible sulfur chemistry from stringent mechanical confinement.

title: A Sustainable, Robust, Soft-Gated Janus Bio-Membrane for High-Flux Aromatic Recovery From Saline Industrial Wastewaters.
abstract: NA: The selective recovery of aromatic pollutants from saline wastewater remains a central challenge in sustainable chemical engineering. We present a bio-derived Janus membrane that couples a sorption-active, mechanically robust wood scaffold with an ultrathin polydimethylsiloxane (PDMS) layer for soft-gated aromatic transport. Spectroscopic, molecular, and free-volume analyses support transient hydroxyl-mediated phenol capture, favorable interfacial association, and onward diffusion through PDMS. The membrane achieves an overall phenol mass-transfer coefficient of 36.9 × 10-7 m s-1 and 99.4% salt rejection under ambient conditions, with sustained performance in petrochemical and offshore oilfield wastewaters. It combines a tensile strength of ∼70 MPa with consistent separation performance across a meter-long sheet. Life-cycle and national-scale analyses indicate over 85% reductions in environmental impact and over 42 000 tons of CO2-equivalent mitigation annually. This work establishes a scalable bio-derived membrane architecture that bridges molecular transport design with aromatic resource recovery, advancing the valorization of saline industrial wastewaters.

title: Realizing Reversible Photo-Charging via Stacked 1T/2H MoS2 Bifunctional Cathodes for Photo-Rechargeable Batteries.
abstract: NA: Photo-rechargeable batteries that integrate solar energy harvesting, conversion, and storage in a single device are able to efficiently utilize sustainable energy. However, current photo-batteries based on bifunctional (photovoltaic conversion and energy storage) cathodes could only achieve photo-assisted charging, whereas light-only photo-charging remains incomplete and irreversible. Particularly, in absence of a photo-charging circuit, the observed charging phenomena are pseudo photo-charging due to side reactions. To realize genuine photo-charging, we design a bifunctional cathode of MoS2 by integrating photo active (2H) and energy storage (1T) phases. Nickel oxide is introduced to improve the interface conductivity and stabilize the 2H/1T phases of MoS2. Additionally, we employed an external resistance to balance the self-discharge current and the photo-charging current under illumination. For the first time, we demonstrate Zn2+ photo-batteries that can be reversibly photo-charged for over ten times, and the deposition of zinc at the anode is visualized. The photo-rechargeable batteries could realize a photo-charging capacity ratio of 100% by 2 h illumination, with a specific capacity of 110.55 mAh g-1. Furthermore, we assemble a sustainable energy harvest-conversion-storage mini-system that could practically provide energy to portable electronics.

title: Submolecular Selenium Enables Low-Pressure and Recyclable All-Solid-State Li-Se Batteries.
abstract: NA: All-solid-state lithium-selenium (Li-Se) batteries offer high energy density and intrinsic safety, but their practical deployment is hindered by sluggish solid-state redox kinetics, large volume fluctuations, and unstable solid-solid interfaces, particularly under low stack pressure. Here we report a submolecular Sex cathode by converting crystalline cyclo-Se8 into amorphous single-atom and short-chain Se (Sex, x < 4) species anchored on graphene (Sex@G), which increases the electronic conductivity from 6.3 × 10-5 to 13 S cm-1 and Li+ diffusivity from 1.7 × 10-14 to 2.0 × 10-11 cm2 s-1. Meanwhile, a Li2O-nanoshell-modified sulfide solid electrolyte is designed to stabilize the interface against both Li metal and Se cathode. As a result, all-solid-state Li-Se batteries deliver the theoretical capacity of 673 mAh g-1 at 0.1 C and retain 86% capacity over 2800 cycles at 3 C under 8 MPa, with stable operation down to -30°C. All-solid-state Li-Se pouch cells further achieve an energy density of 420 Wh kg-1 and 94% capacity retention after 300 cycles under 2.5 MPa. Post-mortem analysis reveals that the submolecular Sex species are not only structurally preserved but also recyclable after electrochemical cycling within the solid-state reaction environment. This work establishes submolecular chalcogen chemistry as a new design paradigm for low-pressure, recyclable, and high-energy all-solid-state batteries.

title: A Device-to-Package Perspective on Thermal Management Materials for Electronic Devices.
abstract: NA: With the continued miniaturization and integration of electronic devices, power density and local heat flux have increased substantially, making heat dissipation a major constraint on device performance and reliability. Improving thermal transport inside devices through materials engineering has therefore attracted increasing attention. In this review, we systematically summarize the thermal transport mechanisms, recent progress, and manipulation strategies of materials for thermal management of electronic devices along the internal heat-dissipation pathway. At the device and die level, we discuss representative semiconductors, metals, and dielectrics, with emphasis on their thermal transport mechanisms and their thermal conductivity manipulation. In addition, thermal transport across microscopic interfaces is discussed.
