The targeted TALE LNP exhibits a base editing effect, cancer targeting, and remarkable therapy efficacy in NSCLC cancer-bearing mice. In conclusion, the targeted TALE LNP has the potential to treat lung cancer with KRAS gene mutation through an approach of transcription activator-like effector base editing.

title: Piezoelectric electroporation potentiates high-frequency irreversible electroporation for enhanced prostate cancer eradication.
abstract: NA: Residual tumor cell persistence remains a critical unresolved barrier limiting focal therapy such as high-frequency irreversible electroporation (H-FIRE) for prostate cancer. In this study, we identified DNA damage repair as the central mechanism governing the reversible survival of residual cells after H-FIRE. By exploiting the transient membrane permeability of these residual cells following H-FIRE, we engineered a piezoelectrically active nanomaterial, BOIS. Exogenous electric pulses generated by H-FIRE enhance tumor membrane permeabilization, thereby facilitating the intracellular delivery of BOIS and promoting its efficient penetration into residual malignant cells. Upon ultrasound activation, BOIS induces surface charge separation and electron migration, producing an intrinsic electric field accompanied by reactive oxygen species (ROS). This dual mechanism cascade simultaneously inflicts endogenous electric field-mediated electroporation damage on both cellular and nuclear membranes and imposes lethal oxidative stress, thereby converting reversibly injured residual cells into an irreversible death trajectory. Consequently, residual tumor cells with damage repair capacity are converted from a reversibly injured state to irreversible lethal damage. Unlike conventional combination therapies, this study pioneered a new therapeutic paradigm in which the focal ablation procedure functions as a nanomaterial delivery mechanism, thereby establishing a self-reinforcing therapeutic loop. This strategy markedly amplified the therapeutic efficacy of H-FIRE and enhanced the eradication of residual tumor cells. Collectively, these findings establish a groundbreaking therapeutic paradigm for eliminating residual disease following focal ablation.

title: Programming a pro-regenerative microenvironment via a photocurable albumin-matrix hydrogel for hepatic tissue reconstitution.
abstract: NA: Liver tissue engineering (LTE) is constrained by poor hepatocyte survival and functional deterioration after transplantation. A central challenge is to support hepatocyte growth and expansion in vitro while preserving polarity and specialized hepatic functions. Graft immunogenicity and surgical intervention trigger inflammation and immune rejection, further compromising transplanted cell survival and performance. Limited vascularization also restricts graft survival, function, and expansion in vivo. Here, we developed a photocurable biomimetic composite hydrogel by combining bovine serum albumin methacrylate (BSA-MA) with decellularized liver extracellular matrix (dECM) derived from α1,3-galactosyltransferase knockout (GTKO) Bama miniature pigs, and used it to encapsulate primary hepatocyte spheroids to construct functional engineered hepatic tissue (EHT). The BSA-MA-dECM hydrogel exhibited favorable physicochemical properties, cytocompatibility, and histocompatibility, while sustaining and enhancing hepatocyte viability, function, and polarity. It also reduced inflammatory responses, promoted macrophage polarization toward the M2 phenotype, and stimulated angiogenesis through VEGF and FGF upregulation as well as PI3K-AKT pathway activation. Thus, the hydrogel established a pro-regenerative microenvironment that supported hepatocyte expansion and graft vascularization. Following implantation into the omentum of rats with CCl4-induced liver injury, the EHT underwent rapid vascularization and showed robust expansion in vivo. It alleviated liver injury, collagen deposition, and fibrosis, while transcriptomic analysis revealed enhanced metabolic repair and cytoprotective programs along with the suppression of inflammatory and fibrotic pathways. Overall, these findings identify BSA-MA-dECM as a versatile photocurable hydrogel for hepatocyte delivery and provide a broadly applicable strategy that integrates immune modulation with vascular induction for scalable EHT construction and liver regenerative therapy.

title: Balancing localized and charge-transfer excited states in Dithieno[3,2-b:2',3'-d]pyrrole-based NIR-II AIE photosensitizers for low power phototheranostics.
abstract: NA: Photodynamic therapy (PDT) is limited by the shallow tissue penetration of visible-light excitation and the hypoxic tumor microenvironment, while effective photothermal therapy (PTT) and PDT/PTT synergistic therapy remain difficult to achieve under clinically approved laser power. Here, we report a progressive donor-acceptor (D-A) intensification strategy that, counterintuitively, reveals a critical excited-state phase transition from a charge-transfer (CT)-dominated regime to a balanced localized-excitation (LE)/CT hybrid. At this tipping point, the inherent orthogonality between radiative decay, intersystem crossing, and thermal dissipation is synergistically breached. This process concurrently unlocks NIR-II emission, oxygen-independent Type-I photodynamic activity, and an exceptional photothermal conversion efficiency of 87.4%. Such tri-functional synergy is conspicuously absent in conventional D-A systems with either weak or excessive D-A interactions. Quantitative structure-property relationship analysis establishes the LE/CT composition ratio as a predictive descriptor for triplet-state reactivity, enabling rational rather than trial and error optimization. Guided by this paradigm, the optimal photosensitizer achieves potent antitumor efficacy under mild 808 nm irradiation (0.33 W/cm2), effectively decoupling therapeutic potency from reliance on high-intensity laser exposure. This work thus shifts phototheranostic design from discrete molecular screening to excited-state composition engineering, offering a conceptually transformative roadmap for safe and efficient NIR-II phototheranostics.

title: Cell-enriched granular bioinks enable vascular integration and endometrial repair.
abstract: NA: 3D bioprinting is essential for constructing functional tissue mimics but remains challenging due to the difficulty of simultaneously achieving adequate cell-cell interactions and appropriate biomaterial support. Here, we introduce a cell-driven clustering strategy that assembles hydrogel microparticles into cell-rich aggregates, in which cells occupy the interstitial spaces and establish pre-organized cellular interactions prior to printing. The cell volume fraction and aggregate size are tunable by microparticle properties and cell type. When applied to digital light processing 3D bioprinting, the cell-clustered granular bioink exhibits high printability while maintaining high cell density and viability. Importantly, preserving pre-established cellular organization translates into enhanced function, including improved stemness maintenance and a more regenerative paracrine profile characterized by increased angiogenic factor secretion and reduced inflammatory signaling. In vivo, implanted constructs show improved cell retention, successful vascular integration with host circulation, and significantly enhanced endometrial repair with reduced fibrosis. These results establish cell-clustered granular bioinks as a generalizable biofabrication strategy for engineering transplantable artificial tissues.

title: An injectable ROS-responsive natural drug self-delivery hydrogel relieves neuropathic pain by remodeling DRG macrophage-mediated neuroinflammation.
abstract: NA: Neuropathic pain remains a major clinical challenge owing to complex neuroimmune mechanisms and limited disease-modifying therapies. Neuroinflammation within the dorsal root ganglion (DRG), particularly macrophage infiltration and pro-inflammatory polarization, is a key driver of sensory neuronal sensitization and pain persistence. Here, we report an injectable reactive oxygen species (ROS)-responsive natural drug self-delivery hydrogel for localized and sustained treatment of neuropathic pain. Single-cell transcriptomic reanalysis revealed marked macrophage accumulation in injured DRGs, accompanied by M1-like polarization and aberrant phosphatidylinositol 3-kinase (PI3K)-Akt activation. Mechanism-guided virtual screening identified glycyrrhizic acid (GA), a bioactive natural product, as a promising PI3K-targeting candidate. To improve local bioavailability, GA was engineered into a 1,4-phenylenediboronic acid (1,4-PBA)-functionalized self-assembled hydrogel, termed GA-PBA-GA (GPG), through dynamic boronate ester bonds and non-covalent interactions. The GPG hydrogel exhibited injectability, self-healing, biodegradability, biocompatibility, and inflammation-associated ROS-triggered GA release. In vitro, GPG suppressed PI3K-Akt signaling, reduced pro-inflammatory macrophage activation, and promoted M1-to-M2 repolarization. In a rat model of L5 spinal nerve ligation-induced neuropathic pain, peri-DRG administration alleviated mechanical and thermal hypersensitivity, improved gait and electrophysiological function, reduced DRG macrophage-mediated neuroinflammation, and attenuated spinal microglial activation. This ROS-responsive natural drug self-delivery hydrogel provides a minimally invasive strategy for remodeling DRG neuroinflammation and achieving sustained relief of neuropathic pain through localized drug delivery.

title: Magnesium-loaded anisotropic hydrogel promotes tendon healing via combined immunomodulation and collagen remodeling.
abstract: NA: Poor tendon healing remains a challenging clinical problem. An ideal repair scaffold should create a favorable microenvironment for dynamic regeneration, including inflammation control, cell proliferation promotion, revascularization, and collagen remodeling. Herein, a dynamic self-adaptive hydrogel scaffold was developed using non-covalent crosslinking and pre-stretching-induced alignment. This biomimetic scaffold integrates tendon-inspired anisotropic surface topography, excellent mechanical properties, anti-inflammatory capacity, and a bioactive ion release gradient, enabling rapid construction of a favorable regenerative microenvironment. In vitro experiments confirmed that the scaffold significantly reduced TNF-α secretion, inhibited macrophage polarization toward the M1 phenotype, promoted the migration, proliferation, and differentiation of tendon stem cells (TSPCs), and enhanced endothelial cell migration, tube formation, and angiogenic factor expression. Meanwhile, in vivo results further demonstrated that the magnesium ion (Mg2+)-loaded anisotropic scaffold significantly increased the M2 macrophages proportion and IL-10 expression, while markedly reducing tissue adhesion. Moreover, endogenous tendon regeneration was significantly enhanced, as evidenced by activation of the HIF1-α/VEGF pathway, a clearly visible vascular network within the tissue, significantly improved proliferation and differentiation capabilities of TSPCs, abundant and well-aligned collagen expression, and substantially enhanced mechanical properties. By integrating the physiological tendon regeneration processes, this biomimetic multifunctional scaffold offers a promising strategy for accelerating tendon regeneration.

title: Bioactive shape-memory biodegradable biliary stent functionalized with dHAM-Curcumin for improved biliary repair and microenvironment modulation.
abstract: NA: Anastomotic stricture after biliodigestive reconstruction remains a clinical challenge leading to recurrent cholangitis, jaundice, and secondary biliary cirrhosis. Conventional plastic stents provide temporary support but are prone to biofilm formation and biliary sludge accumulation and require secondary removal procedures. There is a need for biodegradable biliary stents that provide sufficient mechanical support while actively modulating the local microenvironment. A biodegradable shape-memory biliary stent composed of a poly(CL-co-TOSUO)/BaSO4 (PCT/BaSO4) composite core coated with a decellularized human amniotic membrane-curcumin (dHAM-Cur) hydrogel was developed. In vivo performance was assessed in rat subcutaneous and duodenal implantation models and in a rabbit orthotopic common bile duct stenting model. Gut microbiota and bile metabolomic changes were analyzed by 16S rRNA sequencing and untargeted Liquid Chromatography-Mass Spectrometry (LC-MS). The PCT/BaSO4 stent exhibited suitable mechanical properties, radiopacity, and shape memory functionality, with a degradation profile that matched the expected biliary healing period. The dHAM-Cur coating increased surface hydrophilicity and supported sustained curcumin release. The functionalized stent reduced inflammatory cell infiltration, fibrous capsule formation, and bile duct fibrosis, and preserved biliary patency compared with plastic and PCL/BaSO4 controls in vivo. Multi-omics analyses suggested that the stent subtly reshaped gut microbial composition and modulated bile acid-related metabolic pathways. The PCT/BaSO4@dHAM-Cur composite demonstrated local anti-inflammatory and anti-adhesion effects in preclinical models, along with favorable biocompatibility and anti-restenotic potential. This system holds promise as a therapeutic platform for the clinical management of biliodigestive anastomoses.

title: Cytochalasin D-induced cytoskeletal remodeling with MYH9 enhances release of extracellular vesicles for therapeutic application.
abstract: NA: Extracellular vesicles (EVs) hold great potential as therapeutic vehicles, but their clinical application is limited by low production yields. Here, we explored whether the pharmacological disruption of the actin cytoskeleton using cytochalasin D (CytoD) could enhance EV release while maintaining properties essential for therapeutic use. We examined monocytic U937 cells and colorectal cancer SW480 cells, discovering that CytoD increased EV production by approximately 8.27-fold in U937 cells and 10.06-fold in SW480 cells, while largely preserving the size distribution and surface charge of the EVs. Density gradient ultracentrifugation and label-free quantitative proteomics revealed that CytoD not only increased overall EV release but also selectively remodeled EV proteins. Notably, CytoD-EVs retained lineage-associated membrane proteins such as LFA-1 and showed an enrichment of cytoskeleton-related regulators, particularly MYH9, as well as proteins involved in adhesion and membrane trafficking. We observed the recruitment of MYH9 to membrane blebs,and both pharmacological inhibition with blebbistatin and MYH9 knockdown suppressed EV release, indicating that actomyosin-dependent contractility stimulates EV shedding. Importantly, CytoD-EVs proved to be highly effective drug carriers that doxorubicin-loaded EVs efficiently delivered cargo to recipient cells and induced greater cytotoxicity than free doxorubicin at equivalent doses. Overall, these findings demonstrate that CytoD-induced cytoskeletal remodeling enhances EV production through MYH9-associated membrane dynamics while preserving their capacity for therapeutic delivery. Thus, our findings establish CytoD-induced EV biogenesis as a robust, scalable, and translationally applicable platform for advanced EV-based drug delivery systems.

title: Achieving the targeted retention of nanomotors via a controllable "braking" mechanism based on molecularly programmed engine disassembly.
abstract: NA: Nanomotors have unique autonomous mobility capabilities, offering significant advantages for promoting deep penetration of drugs into pathological sites. However, achieving on-demand "braking" and active retention within target areas remains a critical challenge for efficient, intelligent delivery. The absence of controllable braking mechanisms may cause the nanomotor to continue moving and rapidly dissipate after reaching the target site, hindering effective local enrichment and sustained therapy. In this study, a peptide nucleic acid (PNA)-triggered, in vivo-controlled, engine-disassembly-based active braking mechanism is proposed for nanomotors. This nanomotor anchors the different catalytic engine (catalase, urease, glucose oxidase, and Pt) to the carrier surface via programmable PNA complementary, thus accommodating various application scenarios. After reaching the target area and achieving deep penetration, the injected exogenous complementary chains competitively displace the engine, triggering precise "braking." This braking mechanism relies on PNA sequence-specific base-complementary pairing and competitive displacement, enabling on-demand braking in vivo. Experimental results demonstrate that the drug-loaded nanomotor exhibits excellent tumor-targeting accumulation and tissue penetration capabilities in tumor-bearing mouse models. Following the intravenous injection of PNA to trigger braking, it produces the strongest tumor suppression effect. This study provides a novel strategy for developing intelligent nanomotor therapeutic systems that combine deep penetration with long-lasting retention capabilities.

title: Reprogramming tumor vasculature: Integrating normalization biology with vascularized tumor-on-chip models.
abstract: NA: Abnormal tumor vasculature is a hallmark of the tumor microenvironment that promotes hypoxia, therapeutic resistance, and disease progression while limiting the delivery of anticancer therapy. Although early anti-angiogenic therapies were designed to starve tumors by eliminating their blood supply, excessive vessel pruning often aggravated hypoxia and selected for more aggressive phenotypes. These observations led to the concept of vascular normalization, whereby judicious modulation of angiogenic signaling transiently restores vessel structure and function, improving perfusion, oxygenation, drug delivery, and anti-tumor immunity. In this review, we discuss the mechanisms governing tumor vessel formation, maturation, and dysfunction, and examine therapeutic strategies aimed at normalizing the tumor vasculature. We further highlight the major challenges limiting clinical translation, including the transient and heterogeneous nature of the normalization window, adaptive resistance mechanisms, and the lack of robust tools for longitudinal monitoring. We then integrate vascular normalization biology with vascularized tumor-on-chip platforms, examining how key features of the tumor microenvironment, including tissue architecture, extracellular matrix remodeling, hemodynamic forces, metabolic gradients, and multicellular interactions, can be recreated and quantitatively monitored. We critically evaluate how engineering design, biomaterial selection, vascularization strategies, perfusion, and integrated sensing influence the ability of these platforms to capture vascular normalization and therapeutic responses. By linking the hallmarks of vascular normalization to measurable on-chip phenotypes, vascularized tumor-on-chip systems provide controlled frameworks for investigating resistance mechanisms, optimizing treatment timing, and advancing precision oncology. However, challenges related to physiological fidelity, standardization, scalability, and clinical validation continue to limit their broader translation.

title: On-demand biocatalytic dual oxygen spray reprograms the hypoxia-ferroptosis axis to accelerate chronic wound healing.
abstract: NA: Effective clinical management of chronic hypoxic wounds remains challenging due to persistent hypoxic signaling, oxidative stress, and cellular dysfunction. Hypoxia-induced ferroptosis has recently gained attention as a key molecular driver of impaired healing in chronic wounds such as ischemic and diabetic wounds. Herein, a bioinspired self-oxygenating dual spray incorporating silk fibroin, aloe vera mucilage, and hemoglobin in the primary SAH spray and hydrogen peroxide in the secondary Hp spray is developed. Upon application, the dual oxygenation spray (SAH-Hp) triggers peroxide-responsive instantaneous O2 release through the biocatalytic activity of hemoglobin. Localized O2 generation alleviates hypoxia and restores redox and iron homeostasis, thereby interrupting the hypoxia-driven ferroptotic cascade. Mechanistic investigations demonstrate that sustained oxygenation suppresses lipid peroxidation, limits iron overload, and enhances antioxidant defenses through restoration of the GSH-GPX4 antioxidant defense. Consequently, the SAH-Hp spray promotes angiogenic regeneration and tissue repair under pathological hypoxic conditions. Extensive preclinical validation in rabbit ear ischemic wounds and streptozotocin-induced diabetic wounds confirms accelerated healing accompanied by reduced hypoxic stress and ferroptosis regulation. Collectively, the on-demand SAH-Hp spray facilitates localized O2 generation as an effective strategy for managing chronic wounds by targeting the hypoxia-ferroptosis axis, providing a clinically translatable oxygenation platform for next-generation regenerative wound therapies.

title: A mechanically active microneedle platform integrated with engineered exosomes for enhanced tendon-bone regeneration.
abstract: NA: Functional regeneration of the tendon-bone interface remains a major challenge because early healing is constrained by an adverse inflammatory microenvironment and insufficient mechanical cues. Here, we developed a mechano-regenerative strategy that combines YAP-primed engineered exosomes with localized biomaterial-based delivery and active mechanical stimulation. Exosomes derived from a YAP agonist (PY-60) preconditioned TDSCs (P-Exo) showed enhanced uptake and promoted the osteogenic and chondrogenic differentiation of bone marrow mesenchymal stem cells, accompanied by activation of YAP-associated signaling and PI3K-Akt-related pathways. To improve local retention, P-Exo were incorporated into a ROS-responsive adhesive hydrogel, which accelerated fibrocartilage formation, bone ingrowth, and biomechanical restoration in a rabbit tendon-bone healing model. To address more complex repair conditions, we engineered a three-layer self-contracting microneedle platform for deep-tissue delivery of P-Exo with concurrent active mechanical stimulation. In an infected rat rotator cuff model, this system reduced bacterial burden and oxidative stress, promoted a reparative macrophage polarization and angiogenesis, and improved tendon-bone structural regeneration, biomechanical strength, and functional recovery. Together, these findings support a therapeutic framework in which engineered exosome signaling and active mechanoregulation act in concert to enhance tendon-bone repair.

title: Hybrid nanovesicle artificial antigen-presenting cells integrate endogenous tumor antigen display with senescence-mimetic erythrocyte membrane-directed splenic T-cell priming.
abstract: NA: Artificial antigen-presenting cells (aAPCs) provide a non-genetic approach to T-cell activation, but their in vivo performance is often limited by predefined peptide-major histocompatibility complex class I (pMHC-I) repertoires and inefficient delivery to secondary lymphoid organs. Here, we engineer senescence-derived hybrid nanovesicles that integrate endogenous antigen display and organ-directed trafficking within a single membrane material. Nanovesicles derived from senescent cancer cells retain increased levels of endogenously generated pMHC-I complexes, whereas nanovesicles derived from senescence-mimetic red blood cells confer spleen-directed biodistribution. Fusion of these membranes generates SS-hNVs, which are further functionalized with anti-CD28 and interleukin-2 to form SS-aAPCs that provide coordinated T-cell receptor (TCR), costimulatory, and cytokine signals. Hybrid membrane composition governs splenic accumulation and CD8+ T-cell engagement following intravenous administration. SS-aAPCs expand antigen-specific CD8+ T cells and TCF-1+PD-1+ progenitor-like populations, enhance cytotoxic responses, and suppress tumor growth in B16-OVA and MC38 models. Combination with programmed death-ligand 1 (PD-L1) blockade further improves tumor control. By assigning endogenous antigen display and lymphoid trafficking to distinct source membranes, this platform establishes a structure-function strategy for constructing systemically administered aAPCs. These findings support that physiologically remodeled membranes can be assembled as modular biomaterials to coordinate molecular immune signaling with organ-level biodistribution, enabling in vivo T-cell priming without predefined epitope loading or genetic modification of immune cells.

title: Programming hemostasis and healing via charge-density modulation in a thermo-responsive hydrogel.
abstract: NA: Uncontrolled bleeding and impaired healing are two interlinked challenges in wound management. Here, we introduce charge-density modulation of polymers as a universal design strategy to program biointerfaces that actively promote both hemostasis and healing. By tuning the cationic density of ε-polylysine, we develop an intermediate variant (EPL-C2) that preferentially interacts with fibrinogen over abundant plasma-protein competitors, as supported by protein-adsorption assays, LC-MS/MS analysis, and isothermal titration calorimetry. Incorporating EPL-C2 into a thermo-responsive hydrogel (FN-C2) creates a hemostatic interface that enhances fibrinogen adsorption and platelet adhesion while avoiding broad or excessive activation of the plasma coagulation cascade, leading to superior hemostatic performance in vitro and in a severe arterial injury model. A key advantage of this charge-optimized FN-C2 platform is its ability to serve as a matrix for integrated therapeutic delivery without compromising its hemostatic interface. By loading insulin, the obtained FN-C2-I formulation facilitates sustained release and significantly accelerates skin and intestinal wound healing through enhanced granulation tissue formation, collagen deposition, and a pro-healing immune response. This work presents a synergistic structure-function strategy for next-generation wound dressings, in which tailored control of charge density creates a fibrinogen-selective hemostatic interface inherently compatible with integrated therapeutic delivery.

title: Bimetallic biomimetic catalytic STING sensitizer for coordinating innate and adaptive immune responses against biofilm infections.
abstract: NA: Implant-related infections remain refractory because bacterial biofilms create a physical barrier and are accompanied by local immune dysfunction. Here, we develop a biomimetic metallo-immunocatalytic nanoplatform by cloaking a pH-responsive manganese-iron layered double hydroxide (MFH) core with an M1 macrophage membrane to form MFHM. This design integrates a structurally coupled Mn-Fe catalytic lattice with a functionally preserved biointerface, enabling infection-targeted delivery, colloidal stability, and microenvironment-responsive ion release. Within the acidic biofilm niche, the electronically coupled MFH core promotes Fe/Mn redox cycling and sustains Fenton-like reactive oxygen species generation, thereby disrupting extracellular polymeric substances, damaging bacterial membranes, and perturbing bacterial metal homeostasis. Concurrently, released Mn2+ and redox-active Fe species act as immunomodulatory cues that enhance cyclic GMP-AMP synthase-stimulator of interferon genes (cGAS-STING) and nuclear factor κB (NF-κB) signaling, promote pro-inflammatory macrophage polarization and phagocytic function, and facilitate dendritic-cell maturation and downstream adaptive immune engagement. In a methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus implant-associated infection model, MFHM markedly reduces bacterial burden, promotes tissue repair, and elicits a coordinated immune response that may support protective adaptive immunity, without apparent treatment-related systemic toxicity. These findings establish a catalytic-immune framework based on a biomimetic bimetallic nanostructure and highlight its potential therapeutic application in recalcitrant biofilm-associated infections.

title: Spontaneous phase separation-driven Janus hydrogel spatiotemporally orchestrates the fibrotic progression for functional tendon regeneration.
abstract: NA: Postoperative tendon regeneration hinges on the precise spatiotemporal orchestration of fibrotic progression, aberrant fibrogenesis instead drives pathological adhesion formation and impairs functional recovery. However, current strategies often target isolated aspects of fibrotic progression and rely on complex fabrication procedures. Here, we engineer a Janus hydrogel (SPS-JH) via spontaneous phase separation-driven stratification and photopolymerization of methacrylated hyaluronic acid (HAM) and poly(lactide)-b-poly(propylene glycol)-b-poly(lactide) dimethacrylate (PLD). This innate water/oil demixing yields a Janus architecture in which the outer HAM layer establishes a lubricated anti-adhesion interface, while the inner PLD layer confers durable mechanical reinforcement. Critically, the SPS-JH decodes the temporal hierarchy of tendon repair: the MMP-2-degradable HAM layer releases COX-2 siRNA to silence fibroblast hyperactivation during early inflammation, whereas the PLD matrix sustains niclosamide (NEN) release to polarize macrophages during inflammation and suppress fibrogenesis during proliferation. In rats with Achilles tendon injury, SPS-JH reduces peritendinous adhesions and promotes biomechanically competent, functional tendon regeneration. Transcriptomic analysis reveals coordinated activation of mechanotransduction and tissue remodeling programs accompanied by suppressed fibrogenic signaling. This work establishes a structurally minimalist yet biologically sophisticated paradigm wherein spontaneous phase separation coordinates with the dynamic fibrotic progression to enable functional tendon regeneration.

title: Engineering biomaterials to improve cytokine therapies for wound healing.
abstract: NA: Recombinant cytokines have been used as therapeutics for cancers, autoimmune diseases, and infectious diseases, but their application in wound healing and tissue regeneration remains relatively underdeveloped. Short half-lives, narrow therapeutic windows, and a myriad of adverse effects due to pleiotropy and redundancy have limited their clinical use. Biomaterial-based delivery platforms such as hydrogels, particles, and scaffolds have gained traction as engineering strategies to bridge this translational gap. Despite their popularity in preclinical research, the last FDA approved biomaterial-based cytokine therapeutic, becaplermin, was approved in 1997. Unlike reviews that focus on material design alone, we investigate clinical trials from 2012 to present day and look at the barriers and bottlenecks of translating this technology beyond the bench. This review focuses on release kinetics, design parameters, and practical applications of cytokine-loaded hydrogels, particles, and scaffolds to accelerate wound healing and regenerate functional tissue after soft tissue damage. We offer insights about future directions for preclinical testing and further engineering considerations to aid in their translation to clinical care for patients with soft tissue injuries.

title: Thermosensitive and tumor-targeted asparaginase fusion protein enables metabolic-immunotherapy for solid tumors.
abstract: NA: Metabolic therapies targeting tumor amino acid dependence, represented by asparaginase (ASNase), have shown limited efficacy in solid tumors, owing to poor stability, low penetration, and high immunogenicity. Here, we design a thermosensitive tumor-targeted ASNase fusion protein (ASNase-ELP-LHRH) via AlphaFold2, by integrating elastin-like polypeptide (ELP) and luteinizing hormone-releasing hormone (LHRH), to overcome these drawbacks. ELP drives in situ depot formation, extending half-life to ∼400 h (95-fold increase) and reducing anti-ASNase antibody levels 70-fold. LHRH mediates receptor-dependent tumor targeting and deep penetration. ASNase-ELP-LHRH achieves persistent asparagine (Asn) depletion, counteracting metabolic adaptation to induce nutrient starvation and apoptosis. Mechanistically, the construct blocks metastasis by suppressing epithelial-mesenchymal transition through downregulating Twist1 and upregulating E-cadherin, effectively inhibiting lung metastasis for 25 days in triple-negative breast cancer models. We further observed time-dependent changes in CD8+ T-cell effector-marker expression under Asn deprivation, characterized by dynamic alterations in IFN-γ and granzyme B expression. Combined with anti-PD-L1, this achieves a "dual boost" of antitumor immunity, durably inhibiting metastasis for 40 days and extending survival 1.5-fold. The modular ligand-exchangeable platform offers a generalizable strategy for protein optimization and establishes ASNase-ELP-LHRH as a promising metabolic-immunotherapeutic agent for solid tumors, bridging protein engineering, tumor metabolism and cancer immunology.

title: Rare-earth-free magnesium-zinc alloy with controlled biodegradation and biocompatibility for novel biodegradable metallic stent.
abstract: NA: Biodegradable magnesium (Mg) alloy stents offer a transient alternative to permanent metallic implants; however, clinically used WE43 contains rare-earth (RE) elements, raising concerns regarding the long-term biosafety of RE-containing degradation products and their potential tissue accumulation. Here, we investigated two RE-free Mg-Zinc (Zn)-based alloys, MZ01 (Mg-1Zn-0.1Ca) and ZM115 (Mg-1Zn-1.5Mn-0.5Sr), and established a mechanistic cascade linking alloy composition and microstructure to electrochemical analyses revealed alloy-dependent differences in grain structure and interfacial corrosion resistance, with MZ01 exhibiting the highest charge-transfer resistance. In a mouse subcutaneous model, MZ01 showed more uniform degradation, smaller and more rapidly resolving hydrogen gas cavities, and a significantly lower microcrack area fraction at Day 56 than WE43 and ZM115, accompanied by attenuated inflammatory and fibrotic responses. In the rabbit iliac arteries, all stents maintained luminal patency without thrombosis through 56 days, while MZ01 exhibited lower neointimal thickness, lower perivascular apoptosis and late inflammation, and enhanced early endothelialization compared with WE43. Preliminary descriptive porcine coronary implantation further demonstrated the technical feasibility and sustained patency of MZ01 over 56 days. Collectively, these findings define a composition-microstructure-corrosion-cellular response-vascular healing axis and identify MZ01 as a RE-free Mg-Zn alloy with controlled biodegradation and favorable biocompatibility, supporting its further development as a biodegradable cardiovascular scaffold.

title: Self-assembly prodrugs for controlled singlet oxygen release and resistance modulation in deep-tumor photodynamic therapy.
abstract: NA: Photodynamic therapy (PDT) offers spatiotemporally controlled tumor ablation via photosensitizer-mediated singlet oxygen (1O2) generation, yet its application to deep-seated solid tumors remains fundamentally constrained by limited light penetration and tumor hypoxia. Endoperoxides (EPOs), which reversibly capture and release 1O2, offer a promising strategy to overcome these constraints. Nevertheless, existing EPO-based systems suffer from uncontrolled half-life-dependent 1O2 release and inefficient utilization. Moreover, PDT-induced oxidative stress upregulates inducible nitric oxide synthase (iNOS), leading to nitric oxide (NO) overproduction that quenches 1O2 and promote adaptive resistance. Herein, we report a self-assembly nano-prodrug enabling on-demand 1O2 release while suppressing NO-mediated resistance. An amphiphilic prodrug, L-NARG-SS-Py, comprising a 1O2-storing pyridone moiety and an iNOS inhibitor linked via a glutathione-responsive disulfide bond, co-assembles with protoporphyrin IX to form nano-prodrug (PPIX@L-NARG-SS-Py NPs). Upon irradiation, generated 1O2 is captured and stored as EPO intermediates, followed by glutathione-triggered release in tumor microenvironment. Simultaneously, released iNOS inhibitor suppresses NO production, thereby reducing 1O2 quenching and amplifying oxidative damage. In deep-seated pancreatic tumor models, the nano-prodrug achieves potent tumor suppression with minimal systemic toxicity. This work establishes a biologically amplified, light-independent PDT strategy for overcoming physical and adaptive resistance in deep-tissue phototherapy.

title: Genetically engineering mast cells as effectors for targeted cancer cell cytotoxicity.
abstract: NA: Type-I hypersensitivity is a mast cell-mediated degranulation process induced by IgE-antigen recognition. Inspired by this highly specific mechanism, we developed a new cell therapy platform by genetically engineering mouse mast cell line MC/9 to overexpress the cytotoxic proteins perforin and granzyme B (PG-MCs) via lentiviral transduction. In the melanoma model utilizing B16 cells expressing membrane-bound OVA, a polarized degranulation of mast cells towards cancer cells was validated upon the recognition of antigens by anti-OVA IgE. PG-MCs could selectively kill cancer cells via IgE-antigen recognition. The IgE-sensitized PG-MCs administered through an intertumoral route delivered perforin 1 (Prf1) and granzyme B (Gmzb) toward target cells to potentiate anti-tumor efficacy. Moreover, we demonstrated the reprogramming effect of tumor microenvironment by PG-MC-induced hypersensitivity, driving an immune remodeling of the tumor milieu, characterized by the increased lymphocyte infiltration. In addition, this mast cell therapy, in combination with 5- fluorouracil (5-Fu), induced a significant inhibition of tumor growth in a B16-OVA mouse model, which is associated with the depletion of myeloid-derived suppressor cells (MDSCs).

title: Spatial lipidome and transcriptome profiling reveals stratified lipid architecture in human articular cartilage.
abstract: NA: Lipids, as a class of endogenous biomaterials, are essential for regulating tissue properties and homeostasis. Articular cartilage is an anisotropic tissue that exhibits spatially organized tissue functions and lipid metabolism, and its microenvironment is sensitive to lipid-mediated regulation. However, the spatial lipid composition and its functional significance in cartilage pathophysiology remain elusive. In this study, we performed spatial lipidomic and transcriptomic analyses on healthy and diseased human articular cartilage. We demonstrate a layer-dependent lipid composition mainly in the extracellular matrix and chondrocyte region, and the stratified lipid architecture aligns with region-specific gene expression and cellular phenotypes. The tissue near the cartilage surfaces is enriched with phospholipids and genes relevant to matrix secretion and lipid transport, whereas the tissue adjacent to subchondral bone, is featured by lyso-phospholipids and genes related to biomineralization. Moreover, we highlight ceramide (CER)'s role in mediating chondrocyte secretion and its potential protective function in early osteoarthritis (OA), suggesting that location-specific lipid diversity may contribute to the regulation of cartilage function. This study not only advances understanding of cartilage pathophysiology, but also provides a material-level blueprint for developing more biomimetic cartilage engineering strategies.

title: Molecularly nanoengineered dendritic cells for tumor-specific antigen capture and sono-activatable cytokine-mediated immunotherapy.
abstract: NA: Engineering artificial dendritic cells (DCs) holds great promise for cancer immunotherapy, but achieving spatiotemporally controlled multifunctionality within the immunosuppressive tumor microenvironment remains a challenge. Here, we report a chemically engineered, ultrasound (US)-activatable artificial DCs nanosystem (nDC-M) that mimics the DC-mediated T-cell immunity through a rationally designed molecular assembly. The nDC-M integrates three key functional modules including a semiconducting polymer nanoparticle and interleukin-2 (IL-2) crosslinked by hypoxia-cleavable fragment for on-demand cytokine release upon US trigger, a matured DC membrane cloak for tumor cell recognition and a surface-anchored maleimide (MAL) group for covalent antigen capture and presentation. Under US treatment, sonodynamic effect of semiconducting polymer ablates tumors and consumes oxygen to allow breakage of hypoxia-cleavable fragments, leading to IL-2 leakage. This nDC-M exhibits a comprehensive and conferred mimicking functions including tumor cell recognition, antigen presentation and sono-activatable cytokine secretion. In bilateral breast cancer and lung metastasis models, US-driven nDC-M therapy significantly suppresses tumor progression and metastasis. Moreover, combining nDC-M with checkpoint blockade achieves complete eradication of local and distant tumors and establishes long-term immunological memory against recurrence. This work presents a modular and stimuli-responsive artificial DC platform that integrates chemical synthesis, molecular nanoengineering, and function modulation, offering a versatile strategy for cancer immunotherapy.

title: Microneedle-guided ultraviolet phototherapy with local calcipotriol delivery for enhanced psoriasis treatment.
abstract: NA: Narrow-band ultraviolet B (NB-UVB) phototherapy is clinically regarded as a first-line treatment for moderate-to-severe plaque psoriasis owing to its high tolerance, broad applicability and easy affordability. However, the therapeutic efficacy of short-wave UV light is limited by poor penetration through the thickened stratum corneum of psoriatic skin, whereas excessive NB-UVB irradiation may provoke cutaneous photodamage. Moreover, NB-UVB administration necessitates trained personnel and frequent hospital visits, resulting in poor patient compliance. Here, we developed microneedles with high UV transmittance (UVMNs) to enhance the transdermal delivery efficiency of NB-UVB, thereby reducing the required irradiation dosage and mitigating the risk of photodamage without compromising therapeutic effect. A vitamin D analog, calcipotriol, was further coated onto the UVMN patch to augment the overall efficacy of the phototherapeutic regimen. After insertion into the skin, the calcipotriol is released from the dissolvable coating within minutes to suppress keratinocyte proliferation, followed by UVMN-guided NB-UVB therapy for regulation of regulatory T/T helper 17 cell balance as well as inhibition of keratinocyte proliferation. The integration of phototherapy and topical therapy effectively ameliorated symptoms in a psoriatic mouse model.

title: A nanostructured gradient Ta-O-F barrier-reservoir coating on 316L stainless steel coordinates anti-infective and osteoregenerative responses.
abstract: NA: Early-stage bacterial infection and inadequate osseointegration remain major causes of failure of orthopedic 316L stainless steel (316L SS) implants. Fluoride-containing surfaces can provide antibacterial activity and support angiogenic and osteoblastic responses when fluoride exposure is appropriately regulated. However, uncontrolled release may cause burst exposure, compromised cytocompatibility, and limited functional durability. Herein, a nanostructured gradient Ta-O-F coating was constructed on 316L SS by stepwise plasma modification: an outer Ta2O5-rich region served as a corrosion-stable barrier, whereas an underlying fluoride-containing region functioned as an ion reservoir, thereby suppressing burst fluoride release and sustaining subsequent exposure. Compared with monofunctional coatings, TO/TF showed improved corrosion resistance, moderated fluoride release, and retained antibacterial activity against S. aureus and E. coli. Phenotypic and transcriptomic analyses indicated that the antibacterial response was primarily associated with fluoride-mediated membrane damage, oxidative stress, metabolic disturbance, and suppression of translation-related pathways. The Ta2O5-rich surface may provide an additional but relatively weak contribution through corrosion stabilization and favorable surface physicochemical properties. The regulated coating also enhanced endothelial migration and tube formation, while promoting osteoblastic adhesion, proliferation, ALP activity, matrix mineralization, and related gene expression in vitro. In an infected rat implantation model, TO/TF reduced local inflammatory infiltration and bacterial burden relative to unmodified 316L SS, while supporting vascular and osteogenic marker expression and improved peri-implant bone architecture. These findings establish a barrier-reservoir strategy for coordinating early anti-infective protection with subsequent osteoregenerative responses on metallic implants.

title: Cryogenic sintering decellularized tissue particles creates porous scaffolds that support long-term alternative macrophage infiltration in large traumatic injuries.
abstract: NA: Decellularized extracellular matrix (ECM) biomaterials are widely utilized in soft tissue reconstruction, triggering a Type 2 inflammatory response that promotes repair. However, it remains challenging to manipulate the geometry and porosity of native ECM forms, like sheets and particulates, without chemically altering composition. We describe a controlled freeze-drying method to cryogenically sinter ECM particles into large, mechanically stable, porous 3D ECM scaffolds without altering matrix composition. Modulating small intestinal submucosa (SIS) ECM particle concentration (50 to 200 mg/mL) and freezing rate (-30 °C to -196 °C) during sintering enabled control over 3D porosity (934-3476 μm2 pore area). Moderate ECM concentrations (100 mg/mL) and slow freezing rates (-80 °C) created scaffolds with the largest pores and high mechanical stability under large strain (storage modulus 4036 ± 172 Pa). In vivo, scaffolds bridged volumetric muscle and fat pad deficits, with fabrication conditions affecting degradation and immune response between 1 and 18 weeks. Rapid CD206+ macrophage infiltration occurred, particularly in 100 mg/mL -80 °C scaffolds (4752 ± 1773 macrophages/mm2). All ECM forms induced interleukin-4 (Il4) expression during the first 2 weeks (over 10-fold vs untreated), though expression in 100 mg/mL -80 °C scaffolds persisted substantially longer (8 weeks) than non-sintered particles. Small-pored 100 mg/mL -196 °C scaffolds degraded faster and remodeled into adipose tissue after 8 to 18 weeks. This study shows that ECM particulate can be processed into mechanically robust 3D scaffolds with controllable porosity and degradation without altering biochemical composition, influencing Type 2 immune activation and tissue remodeling after volumetric injury.

title: 3D-bioprinted dual-factor nerve conduits promote neurovascular co-regeneration via activation of the PI3K/AKT and MAPK/ERK pathways.
abstract: NA: Peripheral nerve repair across challenging defects remains a major clinical hurdle, partly because conventional nerve guidance conduits fail to reconstruct the neurovascular microenvironment essential for coordinated regeneration. To overcome this, we engineered a 3D-bioprinted multichannel conduit composed of alginate (Alg), gelatin methacryloyl (GelMA), and bacterial nanocellulose (BNC), incorporating separately prepared nerve growth factor (NGF)- and vascular endothelial growth factor (VEGF)-loaded poly(lactic-co-glycolic acid) (PLGA) nanospheres and Schwann-like cells derived from stem cells from human exfoliated deciduous teeth (SC-SHEDs). The conduit was evaluated in a 10-mm rat sciatic nerve defect. Combined NGF/VEGF stimulation was associated with sustained AKT and ERK phosphorylation over the measured in vitro time course, together with changes in mTOR and c-Jun phosphorylation. The selected formulation retained the intended printed geometry, supported short-term cell viability, and enabled sustained release of both factors. Across the 1- and 3-month assessments, the NGF + VEGF + SC-SHED group showed increased microvessel density, stronger S100β- and NF200-associated signals, improved myelin morphometry, better electrophysiological and sensorimotor outcomes, and greater gastrocnemius muscle preservation than the untreated control. The combined conduit generally produced the most favorable outcomes among the engineered groups and approached the autograft group for several endpoints. These findings support further evaluation of this integrated strategy for peripheral nerve reconstruction.

title: Polymeric and metallic occluders for interventional therapy of cardiovascular diseases.
abstract: NA: Interventional therapy has, as a minimally invasive approach, been widely adopted for treating cardiovascular diseases, particularly structural heart disease, where occluders play a pivotal role in transcatheter closure. This paper comprehensively reviews the evolutionary trajectory and emerging frontiers of cardiovascular occluders, beginning with their interventional applications in congenital heart defects (atrial septal defect, ventricular septal defect, patent foramen ovale, and patent ductus arteriosus) and left atrial appendage closure. The focus then shifts to occluder materials and design principles, tracing the progression from early non-degradable metals like stainless steel to the current gold standard, nitinol, whose hyperelasticity enables self-expanding devices. To promote rapid endothelialization on nitinol implants, surface nanocoatings of bioceramics such as titanium nitride have been developed to modulate cell-material interactions. To eliminate risks from permanent metallic implants, biodegradable occluders have emerged as an alternative. The design of biodegradable occluders utilizing medical polymers such as polylactic acid and polydioxanone is illustrated, highlighting structural innovations such as locking strategies to overcome the lack of hyperelasticity. Key considerations including matching degradation rate with tissue regeneration and achieving X-ray visibility are also described. Finally, future perspectives are presented: expanding applications to infants and the elderly, incorporating tissue engineering for in situ regeneration, and leveraging nanotechnology and artificial intelligence to optimize device performance. The ongoing advancement of occluder technologies will propel interventional therapy for structural heart disease toward a safer and more effective treatment.

title: From biomarkers to therapeutic targets: Biomaterial-mediated cfDNA scavenging in inflammation.
abstract: NA: Cell-free DNA (cfDNA) displays disease-dependent changes in abundance, fragmentation, composition, and tissue origin. Beyond serving as a noninvasive biomarker, persistent cfDNA can act as a damage-associated molecular pattern, activating TLR9, cGAS-STING, inflammasome signaling, and thromboinflammation. This review synthesizes advances in cfDNA biology, clinical applications, and therapeutic scavenging across inflammatory diseases. We critically evaluate the extent to which current clinical studies support diagnostic, prognostic, and causal conclusions while considering methodological heterogeneity. Particular emphasis is placed on how biomaterials transform cfDNA recognition into treatment. We trace the evolution from free nucleases and soluble cationic agents to nanostructured platforms that integrate DNA sequestration with retention, degradation, lesion targeting, or immunomodulation. Comparison of cationic polymers, dendrimers, core-shell nanoparticles, hydrogels, microneedles, nanosheets, and nuclease-enabled systems reveals how material architecture governs cfDNA accessibility, stability in biofluids, tissue distribution, and therapeutic efficacy. Localized and stimuli-responsive designs may improve selectivity and reduce systemic toxicity, but most efficacy evidence remains preclinical. Clinical translation therefore requires standardized cfDNA measurement, realistic biofluid testing, rigorous pharmacology, scalable manufacturing, and prospective demonstration that selective cfDNA removal improves outcomes without compromising host defense.

title: A tunable brain-targeted PEGylated ginsenoside Rg1 derivative disrupts the ROS-mediated inflammasome-pyroptosis cascade to ameliorate Alzheimer's cognitive deficits.
abstract: NA: The pathogenic cascade of oxidative stress, neuroinflammation, and pyroptosis serves as a core driving factor in the pathogenesis and progression of Alzheimer's disease (AD). Although ginsenoside Rg1 exhibits pleiotropic neuroprotective activities, its poor blood-brain barrier (BBB) permeability severely hinders its clinical translation. To overcome this limitation, a brain-targeted delivery system was constructed using a covalent conjugation strategy, linking purified Rg1 with rhodamine B-modified polyethylene glycol (PEG) of varying chain lengths (Rg1s-PEG). After screening, the derivative Rg1s-PEG-600 was identified as achieving an optimal balance between hydrophilic stealth properties and steric hindrance, demonstrating enhanced brain accumulation and favorable biosafety profiles. In both in vitro and in vivo models of lipopolysaccharide-induced acute neuroinflammation, Rg1s-PEG-600 attenuated reactive oxygen species (ROS) accumulation, inhibited canonical neuronal pyroptosis mediated by the NLRP1/3 inflammasomes, and significantly ameliorated behavioral deficits and synaptic loss. Furthermore, in chronic 5xFAD transgenic mice, systemic administration of Rg1s-PEG-600 for 12 weeks markedly reversed spatial memory decline, anxiety-like behavior, and synaptic protein depletion. Mechanistic studies further revealed that this targeted nanotherapeutic not only suppressed the ROS-NLRP1 signaling axis and subsequent neuronal pyroptosis in the AD brain but also comprehensively inhibited amyloidogenesis and Tau hyperphosphorylation. This work provides a promising, multitarget nanotherapeutic strategy to overcome BBB limitations and disrupt the complex pathological networks underlying neurodegenerative diseases.

title: Implanted and degradable hydrogel evaporative cooler for regional and repeated mild hypothermia therapy of traumatic brain injury.
abstract: NA: Implantable, regional and repeated mild hypothermia represents a promising therapeutic strategy for traumatic brain injury. Here, we develop a soft, degradable hydrogel microchannel evaporative cooler capable of removing heat through water evaporation in microchannels and achieving focused regional cooling within a short time. Fabricated from degradable hydrogels and using water as the coolant, the cooler shows biocompatibility and tissue adhesion. In vivo intracranial experiments with the cooler adhered on the rat dura mater enabled precise temperature regulation during repeated regional hypothermia (33 ± 0.5 °C, 4 h per day for 3 consecutive days). The treatment conferred neuroprotection and supported neural repair, with therapeutic effects persisting for 14 days. Sustained recovery was associated with increased Nestin+/Ki67+ and Sox2+/Ki67+ cells, along with elevated MAP2/PSD95 co-localization. Additional staining confirmed the presence of Nestin+/GFAP- and Sox2+/GFAP- cell populations, supporting the involvement of progenitor-like cells. At 28 days post-injury, rats receiving treatment exhibited reduced lesion volume, preserved axonal integrity and myelination, and ameliorated cognitive performance. Proteomic profiling performed at day 3 further suggested that repeated hypothermia modulates synaptic plasticity, dampens neuroinflammation, and rescues perturbed energy metabolism, representing a multi-faceted response distinct from single-episode hypothermia. Collectively, these findings highlight the translational potential of this implantable cooling strategy for TBI therapy.

title: Dual immuno-mechanical programming of a biomimetic periosteum for load-bearing bone restoration.
abstract: NA: Age-related cortical bone loss remains a major clinical challenge, as current interventions largely neglect the load-bearing cortex and its periosteal niche. Here, a dual-targeted biomimetic periosteum is engineered by mechanistically decoding how inflammaging and mechanical decline converge to impair periosteal stem/progenitor cell (PSC) function. Aging-associated macrophage polarization toward a pro-inflammatory M1 state suppresses Piezo1 expression in PSCs, whereas reduced mechanical input attenuates Piezo1 activation, jointly leading to defective mechanotransduction and osteogenesis. Guided by this mechanoinflammatory framework, a periosteum-mimetic membrane is rationally designed with two complementary modules. First, 2-N,6-O-sulfated chitosan (26SCS) is incorporated to repolarize macrophages and restore Piezo1 expression in PSCs. Second, electrospun fiber architecture is optimized to identify a diameter range that maximally activates Piezo1-dependent Ca2+ influx and YAP signaling under reduced mechanical conditions. This coordinated immunomodulatory-mechanosensory strategy reinstates PSC osteogenic competence and enhances cortical bone thickness and strength in aged and hindlimb-unloaded models. The regenerative effect is abolished in Prrx1+ Piezo1-deficient mice, confirming the necessity of Piezo1-mediated mechanotransduction. This work integrates immune microenvironment regulation with cell-scale mechanosensitive activation, providing a periosteum-targeted biomaterial strategy for rebuilding load-bearing cortical bone during aging and mechanical disuse.

title: Blood-transforming coating enables hemostasis and vascularized bone re-generation via bioactive gelation.
abstract: NA: Conventional bone repair materials often treat blood as an obstacle through physical isolation or passive hemostasis, overlooking its physiological role in the regenerative cascade. Here, we propose a "Blood-Transforming Coating" concept and engineer a functionalized microsphere system (GM/TCP@PEG). The NHS ester-coated microspheres rapidly crosslink with amino-rich blood components to form a robust hydrogel while covalently anchoring to tissue surfaces, transforming blood into a synergistic component that enhances material function. Structural characterization confirmed the core-shell architecture. In in-vitro experiments, the clotting time of GM/TCP@PEG was 15.43 s. Its clotting efficiency index was 4.79-fold that of uncoated microspheres and 15.8-fold that of commercial Yunnan Baiyao (YM). The clot mass was 1.63-fold higher than uncoated microspheres and 2.35-fold higher than commercial Yunnan Baiyao (YM). The shear strength measured on porcine skin reached 25.35 kPa, which was 5.39-fold that of the control group. The blood-derived hydrogel enabled sustained release of VEGF, PDGF-BB, and TGF-β1, promoting endothelial cell migration and tube formation. In vivo, GM/TCP@PEG microspheres achieved rapid hemostasis in rat liver, tail, and porcine liver/spleen hemorrhage models, and significantly enhanced bone regeneration via early vascularization in a rat critical-sized calvarial defect model. This blood-transforming strategy achieves synergistic hemostasis, adhesion, and pro-repair functions, provide a strategy with application prospects for tissue repair in complex hemorrhagic environments.

title: Catalytic MXene implant interfaces reprogram radiation-induced foreign body response to prevent capsular contracture.
abstract: NA: Radiotherapy markedly exacerbates foreign body response (FBR) to silicone implants, driving capsular fibrosis and contracture, yet actionable interfacial mechanisms remain insufficiently defined. Here, we engineer an implant-centered Ti3C2Tx MXene-modified PDMS coating (APM) to modulate the redox microenvironment at the tissue-implant interface to reprogram radiotherapy-induced FBR. Oxygen plasma activation and 3-aminopropyltriethoxysilane (APTES) silanization enable covalent anchoring of single-layer MXene nanosheets onto PDMS, yielding a conformal APM film with enhanced hydrophilicity, preserved layered MXene architecture, enzyme-mimicking ROS-scavenging activity, and excellent cytocompatibility. Transcriptomic profiling guides the study, revealing the coordinated downregulation of inflammatory and extracellular matrix remodeling pathways. Mechanistically, interfacial redox regulation dampens NF-κB signaling and reduces endothelial ICAM-1 expression, thereby limiting monocyte adhesion and downstream inflammatory amplification. A tri-culture endothelial-macrophage-fibroblast model further demonstrates that MXene interfaces disrupt pro-inflammatory crosstalk and inhibit myofibroblast activation. In a murine peri-implant irradiation model, APM-coated implants preserve a CD31+/ICAM-1-low microvasculature, reduce peri-implant pro-inflammatory macrophage accumulation, and significantly decrease capsular thickness and collagen deposition. Collectively, these findings demonstrate that MXene-based catalytic coatings can disrupt the positive feedback loop between radiation injury and fibrotic capsule formation, offering a mechanistically grounded strategy to mitigate implant-associated fibrosis.

title: Ultrasound-triggered spinal cord-mimetic electroactive hydrogel enables localized bioelectrical modulation and promotes spinal cord injury repair through JNK-mediated autophagy.
abstract: NA: Spinal cord injury (SCI) creates a hostile microenvironment that severely limits neural regeneration and functional recovery. Although bioelectrical modulation has emerged as a promising strategy for SCI repair, existing biomaterials generally provide either passive electrical conduction or stimulus-responsive electrical generation, but rarely integrate both properties within a mechanically compliant scaffold suitable for spinal cord repair. Here, we developed an injectable, remotely activatable electroactive hydrogel (SMT) by integrating conductive MXene nanosheets into a silk fibroin/tannic acid matrix, endowing the scaffold with tissue-matched mechanics, continuous electrical conductivity, and stimulus-responsive electrical output. Upon ultrasound activation, SMT generated localized bioelectrical cues within the lesion site. At the cellular level, SMT exhibited intrinsic antioxidant and anti-inflammatory effects that were further enhanced by ultrasound activation, while SMT + US promoted autophagic flux through Ca2+-dependent JNK signaling. In a rat model of SCI, the ultrasound-activated hydrogel promoted neural tissue repair and remyelination, attenuated reactive gliosis, and improved functional recovery. Collectively, this study presents a remotely activatable electroactive hydrogel for SCI repair and provides a promising strategy for dynamic bioelectrical regulation during SCI repair.

title: Regulating the iron-ROS cycle via electronic structure-engineered nanoregulators for Parkinson's disease therapy.
abstract: NA: Iron-driven reactive oxygen species (ROS) amplification forms a self-sustaining pathological cycle in Parkinson's disease (PD), yet remains difficult to therapeutically interrupt due to the lack of strategies that coordinate metal homeostasis and redox regulation. Here, we report an electronic-structure-engineered nanoregulatory strategy that regulates the iron-ROS cycle rather than passively scavenging ROS. Nitrogen-doped, herbal-derived carbon dots (CD) were rationally constructed to establish a conjugated electronic framework, in which heteroatom-induced electron delocalization defined redox-active sites and governed the coupling between iron chelation and catalytic ROS regulation. This structure-electronic state-function relationship enabled programmable disruption of the iron-ROS feedback loop at its source. Functionally, the nanoregulators achieved low-density lipoprotein receptor-related protein 1 (LRP1)-mediated brain delivery, exhibited efficient central nervous system exposure, and underwent brain clearance via the cerebrospinal fluid pathway. At the cellular level, they restored mitochondrial function, suppressed ferroptosis-associated lipid peroxidation, and reprogramed stress-related pathways toward neuronal survival. Transcriptomic analysis further revealed coordinated regulation of redox, metabolic, and inflammatory networks. In Parkinsonian mice, this strategy reduced iron deposition, preserved dopaminergic neurons, and improved motor function. Integration with levodopa further enabled sustained, disease-modifying neuroprotection.

title: Dynamic tensile conditioning of mesenchymal stem cell-laden auxetic scaffolds for enhanced YAP-dependent miR-30 enrichment in extracellular vesicles for pulmonary fibrosis therapy.
abstract: NA: Mesenchymal stem cell-derived extracellular vesicles are promising for treating pulmonary fibrosis. However, the generation of extracellular vesicles (EVs) bearing potent, specific therapeutic cargo remains a significant clinical challenge. This study aims to demonstrate how a material-instructive strategy can be utilized to engineer cargo-specific EVs by precisely mimicking the physiological breathing motion of the lung microenvironment. A dynamic culture system was developed by combining a photo-crosslinkable lung decellularized extracellular matrix with an auxetic scaffold. Mesenchymal stem cells (MSCs) were cultured on these scaffolds under dynamic stretching. The dynamically conditioned EVs (dEVs) were then collected, and their therapeutic mechanisms and efficacy were evaluated both in vitro and in vivo using bleomycin-treated human pulmonary fibroblasts and a bleomycin-induced rat pulmonary fibrosis model, respectively. Dynamic stretching on auxetic scaffolds enhanced MSC mechanotransduction, as indicated by the upregulation and nuclear accumulation of YAP. This mechanical activation drove a YAP-dependent biogenesis pathway, leading to the selective enrichment of miR-30 in dEVs. In vivo administration of dEVs effectively restored lung architecture and attenuated collagen deposition. Mechanistically, dEV-derived miR-30 exerted dual therapeutic effects by directly inhibiting myofibroblast activation and promoting the macrophage phenotype switch from pro-inflammatory M1 to anti-inflammatory M2. Furthermore, the EVs successfully restored mitochondrial homeostasis in damaged cells, thereby supporting tissue repair. EVs engineered with miR-30 mimics fully recapitulated the potent therapeutic effects of dEVs, significantly outperforming miR-100. This study successfully established an auxetic dECM scaffold-based mechanogenetic platform to engineer cargo-specific EVs. The findings indicate that mechanical priming optimizes EV therapeutic efficacy, highlighting the YAP/miR-30 axis and mitochondrial restoration as key targets for alleviating pulmonary fibrosis.

title: Mechanisms underlying biomaterial-regulated macrophage polarization in bone tissue engineering: From interface sensing to immune microenvironment remodeling.
abstract: NA: Traditional biomaterials commonly trigger a foreign body reaction after implantation, leading to fibrous encapsulation and poor osseointegration. Advances in osteoimmunology have enabled contemporary tissue engineering to redefine biomaterials as active modulators of the osteoimmune microenvironment rather than as passive scaffolds. At the core of this reconceptualization is the targeted control of macrophage polarization to establish an immune environment conducive to bone repair. The plasticity of macrophages reflects the dynamic balance between the M1 pro-inflammatory and M2 pro-regenerative states; this plasticity ultimately determines regenerative outcomes. This review offers a conceptual four-dimensional regulatory framework that extends from extracellular interface sensing to intracellular genome remodeling and progresses from material properties and signaling cascade stratification to mitochondrial reprogramming and non-coding RNA (ncRNA) networks. Within this framework, material interfaces function as platforms for activating, transducing, and integrating bioactive signals. These signals can be externally modulated to reshape intracellular metabolic organization and sustain mitochondrial function. At a finer regulatory tier, ncRNAs modulate signaling pathways to achieve the precise post-transcriptional regulation of gene expression. Central to this model is a bidirectional, spatiotemporally dynamic feedback loop linking intrinsic cellular machinery with extrinsic material systems. Linking material design parameters to dynamic biological responses lays a conceptual foundation for the development of biomaterials capable of the adaptive and programmable regulation of the osteoimmune microenvironment. Future research may focus on the precise temporal control of M1/M2 phenotypic switching and the coordinated presentation of multiple signals, thereby advancing the development of next-generation immunomodulatory biomaterials for bone repair.

title: A self-assembled hydrophobic polymer tagged nanoplatform for membrane protein degradation and immunomodulatory drug delivery.
abstract: NA: Targeted protein degradation (TPD) has emerged as a powerful strategy for eliminating disease-driving proteins, yet its broader application remains constrained by limited target specificity and the lack of integrated therapeutic delivery functions. Here, we report Tri@N, a multimodal polymeric nanoplatform that extends hydrophobic polymer-based TPD to membrane-associated targets while simultaneously enabling immunomodulatory drug delivery. Tri@N is engineered to remain stable during systemic circulation but undergo intracellular disassembly in response to elevated GSH levels. This disassembly exposes hydrophobic polymer segments that function as a hydrophobic polymer tag, promoting EGFR destabilization and degradation through both proteasomal and autophagy-lysosomal pathways. In parallel, Tri@N releases niclosamide (NIC), which suppresses the STAT3/PD-L1 signaling axis. In colorectal cancer models, Tri@N achieved coordinated EGFR degradation and PD-L1 downregulation, resulting in enhanced CD8+ T cell-mediated antitumor immunity and robust tumor suppression in vivo. These findings establish Tri@N as a dual-functional polymeric nanoplatform that integrates hydrophobic polymer tagging-mediated degradation of a membrane protein with therapeutic payload delivery, providing a versatile strategy for multimodal cancer therapy.

title: Biomimetic electroactive nano-heterojunction for vascularized bone regeneration in large segmental load-bearing bone defects via temporal regulation of endogenous functional ions.
abstract: NA: The repair and functional reconstruction of large segmental bone defects in load-bearing regions are extremely difficult, mainly because the body's capacity to recruit endogenous functional ions such as Ca2+, Cu2+, and Mg2+ to facilitate mineralization and vascularization is compromised. Herein, inspired by the bioelectric field-mediated ion regulation in native bone, a biomimetic carbon fiber reinforced polyetherketoneketone (CF/PEEK) scaffold incorporated with a bio-heterojunction was fabricated via 3D printing, liquid-phase chemistry and hydrothermal treatment. The heterojunction composed of 2D nano-MXene and in-situ ZnS quantum dots enriches functional ions on the scaffold surface through an endogenous electric field, thereby remarkably improving its bioactivity. In vitro cell experiments demonstrated that the CF/PEEK biomimetic scaffold promotes cells' osteogenic and angiogenic differentiation through the epidermal growth factor receptor (EGFR)-mediated phosphatidylinositol 3-kinase (PI3K)/protein kinase B (Akt) signaling pathway. In vivo investigations via non-load-bearing lacunar and load-bearing segmental bone defect models verified that the CF/PEEK biomimetic scaffold possesses superior bone and vascular regeneration capacity, enabling rapid vascularized bone regeneration under complex stress conditions through a bone-vessel coupling mechanism. This work offers a novel strategy for repairing load-bearing large segmental bone defects and new insights into designing bioelectric field-guided biomimetic materials.

title: Sub-second dopamine reinforcement shapes juvenile social play.
abstract: NA: Juvenile social play is critical for neurodevelopment, yet the neural mechanisms organizing moment-to-moment interactions remain elusive. Using social behavior sequencing (Social-seq)-an occlusion-robust 3D pose estimation and unsupervised clustering pipeline-we found that nucleus accumbens (NAc) dopamine was tightly coupled to sub-second social syllables during naturalistic interactions. In wild-type juveniles, males exhibited a sharper dopaminergic contrast between proactive play and forced submission than females did, consistent with sex-divergent play strategies. In Shank3-deficient autism models, this process was fundamentally corrupted: proactive play-evoked dopamine responses were abolished in males and significantly sign-inverted in females, with male-specific enhancements during non-social behaviors, driving social play deficits. A multi-agent reinforcement learning model parameterized by disrupted, play-related dopaminergic reinforcement values recapitulated mutant phenotypes. Closed-loop optogenetic stimulation of ventral tegmental area (VTA)-NAc dopamine projections, time-locked to proactive play, restored reciprocal play in Shank3-deficient rats. Sub-second dopaminergic reinforcement thus orchestrates naturalistic social behavior, providing a behaviorally contingent interventional framework for neurodevelopmental disorders.

title: Harmonized brain ontology and 3D atlases for human, macaque, and marmoset basal ganglia.
abstract: NA: A major goal of the BRAIN Initiative Cell Atlas Network (BICAN) is to create a suite of foundational reference cell atlases and associated standards for human and nonhuman primate brains. Central to this goal is the creation of cross-species-harmonized cellular taxonomies and structural parcellations with formal ontologies that can be mapped onto 3D reference frameworks, bridging neuroimaging and cellular and histological resolutions. We describe an iterative approach, focused initially on the basal ganglia, to co-create structural and cellular ontologies for human, macaque, and marmoset brains and to map and refine structural parcellations into neuroimaging-based common coordinate frameworks. We create a Harmonized Ontology of Mammalian Brain Anatomy (HOMBA) to meet these needs. These references provide the framework for documenting and mapping all experimental sampling in BICAN, allowing analyses of cellular and molecular variation as a function of topographic position and enabling comparisons of cellular, molecular, and neuroimaging-based functional variation across species.

title: An integrative single-cell epigenomic atlas annotates the regulatory genome of the adult mouse brain.
abstract: NA: Histone modifications underpin the cell-type-specific gene regulatory programs that drive the remarkable cellular diversity of the mammalian brain. Here, we jointly profiled four histone modifications and the transcriptome in 2.5 million nuclei from the adult mouse brain. By integrating these data with chromatin accessibility, DNA methylation, and three-dimensional genome organization, we constructed a unified epigenomic atlas spanning over 100 brain cell subclasses and assigned active, primed, and repressive chromatin states across 81% of the genome. Active chromatin states marked by combinatorial histone modifications better nominate candidate enhancers with functional support than chromatin accessibility alone, while H3K27me3- and H3K9me3-marked chromatin states delineate distinct modes of cell-type-specific gene repression. Finally, this multimodal resource enables the development of deep learning models that predict cell-type-specific epigenomic features and gene expression from DNA sequence, providing a comprehensive framework for annotating the brain regulatory genome and interpreting non-coding disease risk variants.

title: Single-cell, multi-region profiling of the macaque brain across the lifespan.
abstract: NA: Brain aging is a complex process with profound health and societal consequences. However, the molecular and cellular pathways that govern its progression, and inter- and intra-individual variation, remain poorly defined. We present a transcriptomic atlas of 5.3 million cells from 582 samples spanning 11 brain regions of 55 rhesus macaques (aged 0.5-21 years). We identify age-depleted and vulnerable neuronal populations and subtle, age-associated compositional differences in glia-detectable only at single-cell resolution. We chart convergent and divergent age-associated molecular signatures across regions and cell types, which include sex-specific signatures that could underlie biases in neurological disorders. These signatures overlap those of Alzheimer's disease (AD), which suggests that aging and AD share molecular roots that emerge at different ages and in region- and sex-specific windows of vulnerability. This work provides a temporal, regional, and sex-stratified atlas of the aging primate brain, offering insights into cell-type-specific vulnerabilities and regional heterogeneity with translational human relevance.

title: A single-cell and spatial 3D multi-omic atlas of developing human basal ganglia.
abstract: NA: Human basal ganglia (BG) neurons and inhibitory interneurons originate in the ganglionic eminences (GEs), transient structures in the ventral prenatal brain. This study delineates the specification and maturation of GEs and GE-derived neurons using single-nucleus methyl-3C sequencing (snm3C-seq), spatial transcriptomics, and single-molecule chromatin + RNA imaging, and we found heterogeneous temporal progression across GE subregions. Spiny projection neurons (SPNs), the principal cells of the BG, acquire distinct subtypes through synchronized 3D-epigenomic remodeling, in contrast to the asynchronous maturation of other neuron types. Oligodendrocyte differentiation involves a transient short-range chromatin state during infancy, showing that the short-range and long-range chromatin conformations previously linked to terminal glial and neuronal fates can also be transient. The temporal cortex matured epigenomically faster than other cortical regions during this period. Lastly, SPNs were enriched in genetic risk for neuropsychiatric disease. Our study extends findings on unique 3D-epigenomic dynamics during human brain development.

title: Disruption of cell-type-specific molecular programs of striatal spiny projection neurons in autism.
abstract: NA: Rare genetic variants contribute substantially to autism spectrum disorder (ASD), yet the regulatory logic of vulnerable subcortical cells is poorly understood. In a 16p11.2 deletion mouse model, lineage tracing across five brain regions revealed prominent striatal changes. In the human putamen from ASD and neurotypical donors, single-nucleus multi-omics showed transcriptional alterations concentrated in D1 striosome spiny projection neurons (SPNs), affecting synaptic and energy metabolism genes, with altered synapse-supporting programs in astrocytes. Gene regulatory network analysis integrating chromatin accessibility and expression identified EGR1 and EGR3 as key regulators of these programs, with reduced activity in D1 striosome SPNs.
